# Transports and framing

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/concepts/transports-and-framing.html
Section: Concepts

> The two transports, a loopback WebSocket and an in-page port, and the text and binary frames that both carry.

## One protocol, any transport

The same frames run over a loopback WebSocket and over an in-page message port. Every transport is wrapped as a `Link`: a bidirectional, ordered, reliable message pipe that sends strings and bytes. Every layer above it is transport-agnostic.

## Loopback WebSocket

The hub listens on `127.0.0.1`, by default on port 7346. Peers open `ws://127.0.0.1:7346/` with the subprotocol `reins.v1`. The hub MUST:

- bind loopback addresses only and refuse any other bind address;
- reject a socket whose remote address is not loopback;
- reject a request whose `Host` header is not `127.0.0.1`, `localhost` or `[::1]` with the hub's port (the defence against DNS rebinding);
- require the `reins.v1` subprotocol;
- disable per-message compression;
- answer plain HTTP requests with a bare status and no body.

Browsers treat loopback as a secure context, so an `https:` page may open `ws://127.0.0.1`. A browser may put loopback access behind a user permission. The driver treats a blocked connection as an ordinary connect failure and reports it. What browsers do today is in [Browser access to loopback](../reference/security-model.md#browser-access-to-loopback).

## In-page port

A `MessagePort`, or the in-memory `linkPair()`, carries the same frames with strings for text frames and `Uint8Array` for binary frames. An assistant that runs inside the browser uses this to reach a surface with no network at all. See [The in-tab shape](../start/in-tab.md).

## Electron port

An Electron app hosts the broker in its main process and links a window to it over a `MessageChannelMain`. The frames are those of the in-page port. A port ends with its document, so a window that reloads or navigates connects again from the new one.

The main process is the embedding code: it takes the link's origin from the frame the port went to, as Electron reports it, and never from anything the page sent. It gives a port only to the top-level frame of a window the app registered, for the page it was registered for. Code that builds a link itself knows what is at the far end, and may vouch for it; the hub then lists that surface as `verified`.

A hub whose surfaces are all linked in-process may close its socket to surfaces (`surfaceSockets: false`, or `reins-hub --no-surface-sockets`). On such a socket a `hello` with role `surface` is answered `bye {code:"E_ORIGIN"}`, whatever `Origin` header came with it. See [Electron: build Reins into your app](../guides/electron.md).

## Links are bounded

A link queues inbound messages until a handler is assigned, at most 4096 messages and 16 MiB; past either bound it drops the queue and closes. Until a connection has authenticated, the hub holds much less from it: at most 16 messages and 64 KiB.

## Text frames

Text frames are JSON objects with a `t` field:

| `t` | Direction | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `challenge` | hub to peer | The first frame on every connection: the versions the hub speaks and a nonce. |
| `hello` | peer to hub | The peer's version, role, name, nonce and proof. A surface adds its manifest. |
| `welcome` | hub to peer | The session id, the limits, and the hub's proof when the peer authenticated. |
| `req` | either | A request: `{id, m, p}`. |
| `res` | either | The one answer to a request: `{re, ok, r}` or `{re, ok:false, e:{code, msg}}`. |
| `evt` | surface to hub, hub to agent | An event: `{topic, d}`. |
| `flow` | stream receiver to sender | `{ch, credit}`: more units may be sent on a stream. |
| `ping`, `pong` | either | The heartbeat: `{ts}`, echoed back unchanged. |
| `bye` | either | Sent right before closing on purpose: `{code, msg?}`. |

A request and its answer, as they cross a link:

```json
{"t":"req","id":7,"m":"act","p":{"s":"s1","a":"cart.add","args":{"sku":"latte"}}}
```

```json
{"t":"res","re":7,"ok":true,"r":{"result":{"count":1,"total":4.5,"items":["1 latte"]},"rev":12}}
```

Ids count up from 1 per sender per connection. Within a version, receivers ignore unknown fields on frames.

## Binary frames

Binary frames start with a kind byte. The only kind so far, in 0.1 and 0.2 alike, is the pointer frame, `0x01`, which carries points of a live cursor trajectory. Its layout is in [Cursor and the pointer stream](./cursor-and-pointer-stream.md).

## Limits

The defaults, which the hub announces in `welcome`:

| Limit | Default | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `maxText` | 256 KiB | The UTF-8 bytes of one text frame |
| `maxBinary` | 16 KiB | The bytes of one binary frame |
| `heartbeatMs` | 15 000 | Idle time after which a side sends `ping` |
| `reqTimeoutMs` | 15 000 | How long a request waits for its answer |
| `consentTimeoutMs` | 60 000 | Extra time the hub allows a request that waits on a consent prompt |

A size limit applies to a frame after its seal is removed. A size in bytes counts the UTF-8 bytes of text.

## When a frame is wrong

A receiver MUST close with `E_TOO_LARGE` on an oversize frame, and with `E_BAD_FRAME` on a frame that is not valid JSON, has an unknown `t`, or lacks a required field. To close with a code is to send `bye {code}` and then close the transport.

A message too large for the transport to take at all is closed by the transport without a `bye`, with WebSocket close code 1009. The hub's WebSocket accepts the frame limit plus a seal MAC: 44 more characters of text, 32 more bytes of binary.

Decoding validates shape: field presence and primitive types.

## The heartbeat

Either side sends `ping {ts}` after `heartbeatMs` of silence. The answer is `pong {ts}` with the same value. A peer silent for 2.5 × `heartbeatMs` is dropped: 37.5 s with the default.

## Further reading

- [Handshake, authentication and sealed sessions](./handshake.md)
- [Limits](../reference/limits.md): every number in one place.
- [Specification, sections 3 and 4](../reference/specification.md#3-transports)

# Handshake, authentication and sealed sessions

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/concepts/handshake.html
Section: Concepts

> How a peer and the hub prove a shared secret to each other without sending it, and how every message after that carries a MAC bound to the handshake.

## Three frames

```text
hub  → peer   challenge { v:["0.2","0.1"], nonce, hub }
peer → hub    hello     { v, role, name, cnonce, auth?, surface? }
hub  → peer   welcome   { v, session, role, limits, proof? }      or   bye { code }
```

The hub speaks first. `challenge.v` lists the versions it speaks, newest first; the peer names the first one it speaks in `hello.v`, and the hub repeats it in `welcome.v`. No common version is `E_VERSION`. Each link has its own version, and a peer that knows only 0.1 is served as 0.1 ([Protocol versions](../reference/protocol-versions.md)). `nonce` and `cnonce` are 32 random bytes, base64url, fresh per connection.

A peer that sends anything but `hello` first, or takes longer than 5 s, is closed.

## The proof

A peer that holds a key proves it without sending it:

```text
auth.proof = b64url(HMAC-SHA256(key, "reins.v1.auth\n" + role + "\n" + kid + "\n" + nonce + "\n" + cnonce))
```

The key is the UTF-8 bytes of the shared secret and the message the UTF-8 bytes of the string. Secrets are 32 random bytes, base64url. A secret never appears in a URL or a log, and it never crosses the wire.

**The hub proves itself too.** When the peer authenticated, `welcome.proof` is the same HMAC with the context `reins.v1.hub`. A peer that holds a key MUST verify it and close on mismatch. This defeats a process squatting on the hub's port: without the secret it cannot answer.

## When a proof fails

- The hub compares proofs in constant time, answers a failed hello with `bye {code:"E_AUTH"}`, and closes.
- A failed proof is answered after a delay: 200 ms, doubling with each failure in the last minute, up to 3 s. Nothing more the peer sends is kept.
- A correct proof is never delayed and never refused because others failed.
- At most 16 handshakes may be pending or waiting out a delay; further connections are closed with `E_BUSY`.
- Keys shorter than 32 characters are rejected when the hub is configured.

## Sealed sessions

When a peer authenticated with a key, every message after `welcome` is sealed in both directions. A process relaying the connection cannot inject, alter or reorder a message or replay one, and cannot drop one unless it also withholds everything after it in that direction: the next message fails to verify.

Both sides derive one key per direction from the shared secret and the transcript of the handshake:

```text
th = b64url(SHA-256(L(c) || c || L(h) || h || L(w) || w))
k  = HMAC-SHA256(key, context + "\n" + nonce + "\n" + cnonce + "\n" + th)
```

Here c, h and w are the UTF-8 bytes of the `challenge`, `hello` and `welcome` frame texts exactly as sent, and L(x) is the byte length of x as an unsigned 32-bit big-endian integer. The context is `reins.v1.seal.peer` for what the peer sends and `reins.v1.seal.hub` for what the hub sends. The two ends agree on the keys only if both saw the same three frames.

Each direction counts its messages from 0, and the counter is never sent:

```text
mac = HMAC-SHA256(k, u64be(seq) || kind || payload)      kind: 0x74 for text, 0x62 for binary
```

On the wire:

- a sealed **text** message is the base64url MAC (43 characters), `.`, then the text;
- a sealed **binary** message is the bytes followed by the 32 MAC bytes.

A message that does not verify closes the connection and is not delivered. Text that is not well-formed Unicode (it holds a lone surrogate) is never sealed or opened.

The [playground](../../playground.html) shows this live: the assistant's frames are marked `sealed`, and opening one shows its MAC.

### Key confirmation

Right after `welcome` the peer sends a sealed `ping`. The hub answers with a sealed `pong` and only then registers the peer and acts on anything that was in `hello`. The peer treats the session as established only when that `pong` verifies. Either side gives up after 5 s.

### What sealing does not do

Sealing protects integrity, not secrecy. Frames are plain text on `127.0.0.1`: anyone able to capture loopback traffic or relay a connection can read commands and observations. And withholding the last messages of a direction is not detected; neither end notices until the heartbeat drops the silent peer.

## Agents

**Agents MUST authenticate.** Each agent credential has a `kid`, a key, and optional caps:

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `name` | The display name shown to the person. It overrides the name the agent declares. |
| `scopes` | A cap on the scopes this agent may hold. |
| `origins` | Browser origins this agent may connect from. Without it, browser-origin connections are refused. |
| `surfaces` | Surface origin patterns this agent may attach to, and hear about. Without it, any admitted surface. |
| `maxSessions` | Concurrent sessions for this credential. Default 4. |

If the connection carries an `Origin` header, the agent is a browser page, and that origin MUST be listed on the credential, else `E_ORIGIN`.

With one token, two agents are two sessions of one credential: they share its rate limits and its cap on sessions, and the log cannot tell them apart by credential. `reins-hub --agent <kid>=<file>` gives an agent a credential of its own, and the agent names it with `--kid`.

The name shown to users is the credential's `name` when the operator set one, otherwise the name the agent declared, with control characters and the bidirectional marks and overrides removed, cut to 64 code points.

## Surfaces

**Surfaces are identified by origin.** The hub takes the origin from the WebSocket `Origin` header, or from the embedding code for in-page links, and MUST find it in the configured allowlist, else `E_ORIGIN`. Entries are exact origins, `scheme://host:*` for any port, or `*`. `hello.surface.url` MUST have that origin.

### Origins

An origin is compared as text, in one of four forms:

- a **web origin**: `scheme://host`, with `:port` unless the port is the scheme's default;
- **`file://`**: the origin of every `file:` URL, whatever its host and path;
- an **app origin**: `scheme://host` with any other scheme, which is what a page has when an Electron app serves it from a scheme of its own (`app://notes`);
- **`null`**: an opaque origin, as a `data:` URL, a sandboxed frame, or a page on a scheme the browser gives no hosts has.

An implementation computes the origin of a URL by the rule of the specification (`urlOrigin`) and does not take what a URL library reports, which for a `file:` or app-scheme URL is `null` in some engines and not in others.

In an allowlist, an exact entry matches that origin. `scheme://host:*` matches a web or app origin of that scheme and host with any port or none. **`*` matches every web origin and nothing else**: `file://`, an app origin and `null` are admitted only by an entry that names them.

Two entries admit by an origin that countless pages share. `null` is the origin of every sandboxed frame on every website, and `file://` of every local file. The reference hub warns at start when its socket admits either without requiring a surface key. See [Electron: build Reins into your app](../guides/electron.md#what-origin-your-page-has).

A hub may also hold **surface keys** by app id. A surface whose manifest claims an app id the hub holds a key for MUST prove that key; without a proof it is refused with `E_AUTH`. `requireKey` also refuses every surface without a key. See [Surface keys](../guides/surface-keys.md).

A hub MAY pin an app id to a manifest digest and refuse a surface whose manifest differs (`E_DENIED`). Pinning catches a modified build of the app. It does not stop a forger, who can copy the manifest.

## An unverified hub

A surface that holds no key cannot check the hub's proof, so it cannot tell the hub from another process listening on the same port. Such a surface treats the hub as **unverified**: it never accepts an attach silently (the decision is at least `confirm`), and it tells the user so in the consent prompt and in the indicator.

The kiosk profile has nobody to ask, so a kiosk surface MUST hold a key. A link the app built itself, the in-page transport, counts as verified.

## Closing

Either side sends `bye` before closing on purpose. On shutdown the hub sends `bye {code:"OK"}` to every peer.

## For implementers

Fixed inputs and expected outputs for the proofs and for sealing are in the test vectors: [`auth.json`](../implementers/vectors/auth.md) and [`seal.json`](../implementers/vectors/seal.md). The origin of a URL and the allowlist matches are in [`origins.json`](../implementers/vectors/origins.md).

## Further reading

- [Specification, section 5](../reference/specification.md#5-handshake-and-authentication)
- [Threats and what stops them](../reference/security-model.md#threats-and-what-stops-them): T3 to T11 are about this page.

# Manifest and prompt card

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/concepts/manifest-and-prompt-card.html
Section: Concepts

> How a surface describes itself, and the short text rendered from that description that teaches a model to drive the app.

## The manifest

A surface describes itself in `hello.surface.manifest`:

| Field | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `reins` | The protocol version the manifest was written for. |
| `app` | The app's `id`, `name`, `version` and `description`. |
| `actions` | For each action: `name`, `description`, `params` (a schema-lite object), `risk`, `returns`. |
| `views` | Named renderers the app offers for showing data. |
| `state` | Named pieces of app state an agent may read. |
| `exposure` | What the UI tree exposes: `auto`, `annotated` or `none`. |
| `profile` | Which policy profile runs: `open`, `guarded` or `kiosk`. |

You do not write a manifest by hand. The driver builds it from what you registered with `action`, `view` and `state`: see [Make an app drivable](../start/make-an-app-drivable.md).

Names of actions, views and state are dot-separated lowercase identifiers such as `cart.add`. A manifest is at most 64 KiB, 256 actions and 64 views. The hub validates it and computes `digest`, the base64url SHA-256 of its canonical JSON. An agent sees the digest in the surface listing, and a hub can pin an app id to one.

## Canonical JSON

Canonical JSON, which the audit log uses as well, is JSON without whitespace, with object keys sorted by UTF-16 code units, strings and finite numbers written as ECMAScript `JSON.stringify` writes them, other numbers as `null`, and properties whose value is undefined left out. For JSON input this is the serialisation of RFC 8785. A value nested more than 100 levels deep has no canonical JSON.

## The prompt card

The prompt card is the text an assistant is given so it can drive the app. It is rendered from the manifest and is the same wherever it is produced:

```
# Reins surface s1: Brew Kiosk 1.0.0 (brew-kiosk)
Self-service coffee ordering.
origin http://localhost:5173 | profile guarded | scopes observe act cursor show
Prefer actions over ui ops. [confirm] asks the user on screen. [deny] is blocked.

## actions
cart.add(sku: "latte"|"mocha"|"tea", qty?: int 1..9) -> cart totals. Add an item.
order.submit() [confirm]. Place the order.
admin.refund(order: str) [deny]. Refund an order.

## views
chart(title: str, series: [{label: str, value: num}]). Bar chart panel.

## state
cart: items and totals
```

That is the whole briefing. A model that has read it knows what the app is, which scopes it holds, which actions exist with their arguments, which of them will ask the person and which are blocked. The README puts its size at about a thousand characters.

With the agent SDK the card is `handle.card()`. With the MCP adapter and the shell tools it is what `reins_attach` returns.

## How a card is built

Line by line:

1. `# Reins surface`, then the surface id when it is known, then the app's name, its version if there is one, and its id in parentheses.
2. The app description, if any.
3. `origin`, `profile` and `scopes` (the granted scopes, in canonical order), joined by ` | `.
4. The fixed line: `Prefer actions over ui ops. [confirm] asks the user on screen. [deny] is blocked.`
5. For each of actions, views and state that is not empty: an empty line, the heading, and one line per entry in manifest order.

An action line is the name, its signature, ` -> <returns>` if any, ` [<decision>]` unless the decision is `allow`, and `. <description>`. A view line is the name, its signature and the description. A state line is `<name>: <description>`, or the name alone.

Free text is put on one line first: every run of whitespace and control characters becomes one space and the ends are trimmed. So a description cannot break out of its line.

## Signatures

The signature lists the params of an object schema in declaration order inside parentheses; `()` without params. Each is `name: type`, with `?` after the name when it is not required.

| Schema | Written as |
|---|---|
| a string with `enum` | the values as JSON strings joined by a vertical bar: `"latte"` or `"mocha"` |
| string | `str` |
| integer, number | `int`, `num`, with ` a..b` when a range is given (either end may be missing) |
| boolean | `bool` |
| array | `[T]` |
| object | `{name: T, ...}` |

## The decision tag can be optimistic

The decision tag is what policy says for that action. `allow` has no tag.

A manifest names its profile but does not carry policy overrides, so a card rendered on the agent side shows the profile's decision for each risk tier. Where an app overrides single actions, or the hub's policy is stricter, the tag can be more permissive than what happens: the refusal (`E_DENIED`, `E_CONSENT`) is the truth.

The level and the rules the person sets are not on the card either: under `auto` or `bypass` a `[confirm]` action may run unasked, and a rule may block an action that has no tag. See [Permission levels](./permission-levels.md).

## For implementers

The manifest behind the example card, its canonical JSON, its digest and the card are in the test vectors: [`manifest.json`](../implementers/vectors/manifest.md). A card has to match character for character.

## Further reading

- [Writing good actions and risk tiers](../guides/actions-and-risk.md)
- [Specification, section 7](../reference/specification.md#7-manifest-and-prompt-card)

# Grants and scopes

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/concepts/grants-and-scopes.html
Section: Concepts

> What an agent is allowed to do on one page, how it asks, who can narrow the answer, and how a grant ends.

## Scopes

A scope is a kind of thing an agent may do. In canonical order:

| scope | lets the agent |
|---|---|
| `observe` | read the UI tree, visible text and exposed state; subscribe to events |
| `act` | call the app's declared actions |
| `ui` | synthesise clicks, typing, selection, scrolling and keys on exposed elements |
| `cursor` | show and move the virtual cursor. Visual only: it never dispatches input |
| `show` | toasts, highlights, and the app's data views |
| `nav` | open same-origin URLs the policy allows |
| `chat` | talk with the person in the page's chat room: say something, read what was said to it, show what it is doing |

Every method needs one scope: see [Methods](../reference/methods.md). The split between `act` and `ui` matters most. `act` calls actions the app declared, with validated arguments and a risk tier. `ui` synthesises input on whatever is exposed. The kiosk profile has no `ui`, no `nav` and no `chat` at all.

## Attaching

An agent asks for a grant with `surface.attach {s, scopes, reason, tk?}`. Three parties narrow the answer:

1. **The hub** intersects the requested scopes with the agent credential's cap and the hub policy's `scopes`. An empty result is `E_SCOPE`. Hub policy `attach: deny` is `E_DENIED`.
2. The hub sends `attach {agent, scopes, reason, levels, decisions, chatRelay, cred, v, tk?}` to the surface, with `c:1` when the hub policy says `confirm`. `levels` is the list of [permission levels](./permission-levels.md) the hub's policy offers, `decisions` is what the hub's policy decides for each action of the surface's manifest, `chatRelay` is the hub's setting for whether agents hear each other in the [chat](./chat.md), and `cred` is the id of the agent's credential: what stays the same when an agent comes back under another session id or another name. `v` (0.2) is the protocol version the agent's own link speaks, and a ticket (`tk`) is forwarded as the agent sent it ([Requests that wait](./waiting-requests.md)).
3. **The surface** intersects with its own policy and decides by its `attach` setting: `allow`, `confirm` with an on-screen prompt, or `deny`. It answers `{scopes, ttlMs, kept?}`. A refusal is `E_CONSENT` or `E_DENIED`; a request that waits for the person instead is answered `E_WAITING`, with a ticket the agent repeats the attach with once the person has allowed it. `kept`, when present, is what stays of the person's earlier settings for this agent: the level `strict`, rules `confirm` and `deny`, and scopes switched off.
4. The hub records the grant with expiry `min(hub ttl, surface ttl)` and returns `{grant, surface, manifest, kept?}`. `grant.scopes` holds the scopes in force: those granted, without the ones that were kept switched off. `kept` repeats the level and the rules, so that the agent knows from the first moment what it is held to.

So an agent never gets more than its credential, the hub's policy and the page's policy allow, and the scopes it ends up with may be fewer than it asked for. The `reason` is shown to the person in the prompt.

The surface asks the person even when its policy says `allow` if the hub is unverified, or if the user has pressed Stop, or a revocation after refusals has happened, since the page loaded, or if the person has tightened something for an agent that the surface cannot tell this one from (below).

## Attach is bounded

Each attach may put a prompt in front of a person, so it is limited:

- The hub forwards one attach at a time per credential and surface, across all of the credential's sessions. Another gets `E_BUSY`.
- A credential gets a burst of 3 attaches per surface, then one every 2 s. Beyond that: `E_RATE`.
- When an agent session disconnects while its attach is pending, the hub tells the surface, which withdraws the prompt.
- A surface holds at most 32 grants at a time, so that the list a person has to read stays one they can read. It refuses an attach from a further agent with `E_BUSY`, before it asks the person.

## One grant per agent and surface

One agent holds at most one grant per surface. Attaching again replaces it.

A request without a live grant fails with `E_NOT_ATTACHED`. A request whose scope the grant lacks fails with `E_SCOPE`.

## How a grant ends

A grant ends, and the hub tells each side, as follows:

| the grant ends because | the surface gets | the agent gets |
|---|---|---|
| the agent sends `surface.detach` | `detach {why:"agent"}` | the answer `{}` |
| the agent disconnects | `detach {why:"agent"}` | |
| the surface disconnects | | `evt surface {kind:"gone"}`, like every agent that may attach to it |
| it reaches `exp`, or `idleMs` passes without a request | `detach {why:"expired"}` | `evt grant {kind:"expired"}` |
| the surface sends `evt grant {kind:"revoked"}` (Stop, or refusals, section 12), with `ag` for one agent, without for all | | `evt grant {kind:"revoked"}` |
| the surface reports a level that the hub's policy does not offer, more than 20 changes of what the person set within one second, or a change that lets the agent do more while the hub cannot write its audit log (section 13) | `detach {why:"hub"}` | `evt grant {kind:"revoked"}` |
| a new attach by the same agent replaces it | | the new attach result |

Grant lifetimes come from the policy profile: `ttlMs` is the lifetime, and a grant with no request for `idleMs` expires. Under `guarded` that is 2 hours and 15 minutes.

A grant lasts as long as the agent's connection to the hub. That is why the [shell tools](../start/shell-tools.md) keep a small session process: it holds the connection, and the grant, between commands.

## Scope switches

The person can switch single scopes of a live grant off and back on, in the panel that opens from the indicator. The surface refuses a request whose scope is off with `E_SCOPE`, and tells the hub which scopes are now in force. The hub then lets the grant carry only those of the reported scopes that were granted at attach: a report never widens a grant. It tells the agent with `evt grant {kind:"scopes", scopes}`.

When `cursor` goes, that agent's pointer streams are closed and its cursor is hidden. A grant with every scope switched off stays live: the person can switch them back on.

## What ends with a grant, and what stays

**What lets an agent do more ends with the grant.** The levels `auto` and `bypass`, a rule `allow`, a remembered approval and what the person switched on in the chat belong to one grant and end with it, however it ends. A new grant, also one that replaces another for the same agent, has none of them. An agent cannot keep what the person gave an earlier grant by detaching and attaching again. An approval from the [waiting list](./waiting-requests.md) belongs to one grant as well, and an agent's waiting entries end with its grant.

**What the person tightened stays.** The level `strict`, the rules `confirm` and `deny` and the scopes the person switched off hold an agent back, and no sequence of the agent's own calls takes them away: not attaching again, not a detach and a new attach, not letting the grant run out, not coming back under another session id or name. The surface keeps them for as long as the page lives and puts them on every new grant of the same agent, where they are in force from the first request. What the person lifts themselves, in the panel, is no longer kept. The surface says what is kept in its attach answer (`kept`), and the hub starts the grant with it and records it. The hub reads nothing else from an attach answer: no other level, no rule `allow`, no scope that was not granted.

**The same agent** is told by the credential. A surface that got `cred` from a hub it verified keeps what was tightened under that id, and every grant that comes with the same id is the same agent to it, whatever its session id or name. Two credentials are two agents. Where the surface cannot tell (the hub sent no `cred`, or the surface did not verify the hub), every agent is the same agent to it: what the person tightened for one is put on every later grant. Such an attach is never silent: the surface asks the person even where its policy says `allow`, and the prompt says what was set and that it stays.

## Events follow the grant

The hub relays an event only to live grants with the scope its topic needs: `ui`, `state` and `nav` need `observe`, and `user` goes to every live grant. `grant` and `surface` events need no subscription. A `chat` event is never broadcast: it goes to the one grant it names, while that grant holds `chat`. See [Events](../reference/events.md).

## Further reading

- [Policy profiles](./policy-profiles.md)
- [Consent](./consent.md)
- [Specification, section 8](../reference/specification.md#8-grants-and-scopes)

# Policy profiles

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/concepts/policy-profiles.html
Section: Concepts

> The three profiles, open, guarded and kiosk, what each row of their table means, how single actions are overridden, and why a request has to pass two policies.

## A policy is a profile plus overrides

A policy answers one question for everything an agent asks: **allow**, **confirm** or **deny**. `confirm` means the person is asked on screen. The strictness order is allow < confirm < deny.

Three profiles exist:

| | `open` | `guarded` | `kiosk` |
|---|---|---|---|
| intended for | local development | a person's own browser | unattended stations |
| attach | allow | confirm | allow, with a provisioned agent |
| safe / sensitive / dangerous | allow / confirm / confirm | allow / confirm / deny | allow / deny / deny |
| scopes | all | all | observe, act, cursor, show |
| exposure | auto | auto | annotated |
| raw coordinates | yes | yes | no |
| a page inside a frame (`framed`) | refused | refused | refused |
| navigation | same origin | same origin | off |
| user controls | pause, stop | pause, stop | pause |
| levels the person may set (`human.levels`; strict and ask are always on offer) | strict, ask, auto, bypass | strict, ask, auto, bypass | strict, ask |
| the indicator opens the panel (`human.panel`) | yes | yes | no |
| agents hear each other in the chat (`chatRelay`) | `on`: always | `person`: once the person switches it on | `off`: never |
| remember approvals (`consent.remember`) | session | never | never |
| `consent.timeoutMs` | 60 s | 60 s | 30 s |
| a request nobody answered waits (`consent.waitMs`, 0.2) | 10 min | 10 min | no |
| a rule `allow` for a time (`human.allowMs`, 0.2) | 15 min | 15 min | 15 min |
| unasked runs of one action before it asks again (`human.burst`, 0.2) | 60 in 10 min | 20 in 10 min | no cap |
| actions offered at attach (`human.offer`, 0.2) | none | none | none |
| `human.yieldMs` | 600 ms | 800 ms | 400 ms |
| grant `ttlMs` / `idleMs` | 8 h / 30 min | 2 h / 15 min | 8 h / 5 min |
| `rates` per second: observe, act, ui, cursor, show, nav, chat | 30, 30, 60, 120, 30, 2, 10 | 20, 20, 40, 60, 20, 1, 5 | 20, 10, 0, 60, 10, 0, 0 |
| `pointerRate` per second | 4000 | 2000 | 2000 |

- **`open`** is for local development. Everything is reachable, and risky actions still ask. It is the only profile that remembers an approval for the rest of a grant.
- **`guarded`** is the default, for a person's own browser. The person approves every attach and every sensitive action. Dangerous actions are denied. The person can change how much one agent asks, and agents in the chat hear each other only once the person says so.
- **`kiosk`** is for unattended stations, where nobody is there to ask: a fixed allowlist, no synthetic input, no navigation, annotated elements only, no Stop button for visitors, no panel, no level to switch and no chat.

## Reading the table

| Row | Meaning |
|---|---|
| attach | How a request to attach is decided. Under `kiosk` it is allowed for an agent the hub was provisioned with, and the page must hold a surface key. |
| safe / sensitive / dangerous | The decision for an action of each risk tier. |
| scopes | The ceiling on the scopes a grant may carry. |
| exposure | What the UI tree shows: `auto` is interactive elements, headings and the like, plus what is annotated; `annotated` is only what is annotated. |
| raw coordinates | Whether `cursor.move` may take a point, and whether a pointer stream may open. `ui.*` never takes coordinates. |
| a page inside a frame | No profile lets the driver connect inside a frame. An app opts in with `framed: true`. |
| navigation | Whether `nav.go` may open same-origin paths. |
| user controls | Which buttons the indicator has. |
| levels the person may set | Which [permission levels](./permission-levels.md) the panel offers. `strict` and `ask` are always on offer; the kiosk profile offers no other. |
| the indicator opens the panel | Whether the indicator's text is a button that opens the panel with its Permissions, Activity and Chat tabs. |
| agents hear each other in the chat | `chatRelay`: always, once the person switches it on, or never. See [Chat](./chat.md). |
| remember approvals | With `session`, an approved action is not asked again under the same grant. |
| `consent.timeoutMs` | A prompt nobody answers is a refusal after this long. |
| `human.yieldMs` | After real input from the person, input-synthesising commands wait this long. |
| grant `ttlMs` / `idleMs` | The lifetime of a grant, and how long it survives without a request. |
| `rates` | Requests per second by scope, enforced by the hub. A rate of 0 means the scope cannot be used. |
| `pointerRate` | Points per second on pointer streams. |

Every field is described in [Policy fields](../reference/policy-fields.md).

## Choosing and overriding

Pass a profile name, or a profile with overrides. Nested objects merge one level deep.

```js
createDriver({
  app,
  policy: {
    profile: 'guarded',
    nav: [],                              // one page: no agent navigation at all
    actions: {
      'order.refund': 'deny',             // off, whatever its risk tier says
      'cart.*': 'allow',                  // a prefix
    },
    consent: { timeoutMs: 30_000 },
  },
});
```

An unknown field, or a value of the wrong type, is an error when the policy is resolved: a mistyped restriction never means "any".

## How an action is decided

The driver looks for an override in `policy.actions`: the exact name first, then the longest matching `prefix.*`. Without one it uses `policy.risk[action.risk]`.

With the overrides above, `order.refund` is denied, `cart.add` and `cart.clear` are allowed, and `order.submit`, which is `sensitive` and has no override, is `confirm` under `guarded`.

## Two enforcement points

The hub has a policy of its own. A request has to pass both.

The hub evaluates its policy on every request and either refuses, forwards, or forwards with `c:1`, which says that the hub's policy demands a human confirmation. The surface evaluates the app's policy and takes the stricter of its decision, of what the hub said at attach that it decides for the action, and of `c:1`.

Rate limits and grant expiry are the hub's job. Exposure, privacy, frames, consent and human control are the surface's. The person sets levels, rules and scope switches on the surface; the hub caps the levels by its own policy and enforces the scopes. The page enforces its policy by itself, so the app's guardrails hold even behind a misconfigured hub.

Start the hub with a profile, and optionally a configuration file that carries a whole policy object:

```bash
npx --no -- reins-hub --profile kiosk --allow-origin http://localhost:5173
```

## Frames

A page inside a frame is not in charge of what the person sees of it. The page around the frame can cover or overlay any part of it, the consent prompt and the indicator included, and the framed page cannot tell.

A driver whose document is not the top-level document of its tab does not connect to a hub unless the app's policy sets `framed: true`. Its `connect()` fails with `E_DENIED` before anything is sent to the hub or added to the page. No profile sets `framed`. An app that sets it should also say which pages may embed it, with a `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors` header.

An Electron `<webview>` guest is in the same position, and its driver cannot tell: the guest is the top-level document of its own frame tree, while the page that embeds it can draw over it. That check is the main process's.

## See the profiles side by side

The [playground](../../playground.html) runs the same scripted assistant under each profile: switch between `guarded`, `kiosk` and `open` at the top of the page.

## For implementers

The profile table, the override precedence and the strictness order are in the test vectors: [`policy.json`](../implementers/vectors/policy.md).

## Further reading

- [Consent](./consent.md) and [Human control](./human-control.md)
- [Kiosk deployment](../guides/kiosk-deployment.md)
- [Specification, section 12](../reference/specification.md#12-policy)

# Consent

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/concepts/consent.html
Section: Concepts

> The prompt that asks the person before an agent attaches or runs a sensitive action, and the rules that keep an agent from getting a yes it did not earn.

## What a prompt is

When policy answers `confirm`, the driver asks the person on screen. A prompt names the agent, the scopes or the action, and shows the arguments as text. There are two kinds:

- an **attach** prompt: an agent wants to control this page, with the scopes it asks for and its reason;
- an **action** prompt: an agent wants to run an action, with its name, risk tier, description and every argument.

The agent's name is shown inside quotation marks and followed by its session id, as in `“Tab assistant” (a1) wants to control this page`, so that a name cannot pass for words of the page and two agents with one name are told apart.

The prompt lives in a closed shadow root owned by the driver and accepts only trusted input events, so an agent cannot approve its own request: a synthetic click does nothing. That holds against agents and against events a script makes or borrows; it does not hold against script that runs in the page's own JavaScript realm ([Human control](./human-control.md#what-script-in-the-page-can-do)). A prompt has `consent.timeoutMs` for an answer (60 s under `open` and `guarded`, 30 s under `kiosk`).

A refusal reaches the agent as `E_CONSENT`. A prompt nobody answered in time is, in protocol 0.2 and where the request can wait, not a refusal: the request joins the page's waiting list and the agent gets `E_WAITING` with a ticket ([Requests that wait](./waiting-requests.md)). Where it cannot wait (a kiosk, an app's own consent handler, an agent on 0.1, a full list) it is `E_CONSENT`, as before. A request's time runs from when it reached the page, not from when its card is shown, and is never longer than the hub's own wait: a card that waited its turn behind another shows for what is left, and one whose time is up before its turn is not shown at all.

## The third button: Always allow

An action prompt has Deny and, where the request can wait, "Later" on the left, and on the right "Always allow" and Allow, the one filled button; above them one line says what happens if nobody answers ("Goes to the waiting list in 58 s"). Allow approves this one request. "Always allow" also sets the person's rule `allow` for that action and that agent: it will then run without asking, with any arguments, until the agent disconnects.

Because that lets an agent do more, it takes two steps. The first press does not approve anything: the card says what the rule covers, and a second button, armed again after a moment, sets it. The rule shows in the panel, where the person can take it back, and the indicator shows that a rule is waiving a prompt. "Always allow" is offered only where a level on offer would waive the same prompt.

Where the policy has `human.allowMs` above 0 (15 minutes in every profile), that second step also lets the person choose how long the rule holds: until the agent disconnects, which is preselected, or for that time. The button is named by the choice ("Allow for 15 minutes") and armed anew after either choice. A rule for a time ends by the clock, and the indicator says when ("1 rule until 14:05"). See [Permission levels](./permission-levels.md#a-rule-for-a-time).

Whether a prompt appears at all is no longer the policy's decision alone. The person can set an agent to ask every time (`strict`), to stop asking (`auto`, `bypass`), or block a single action, in which case the request fails with `E_CONSENT` ("the user blocked this action") without any prompt. No level and no rule relaxes a policy `deny`.

## What is approved is what runs

The prompt lists every argument in full and shortens nothing: indented JSON, two spaces per level.

- **Invisible and look-alike characters are shown.** Every code point in the Unicode categories C (control, format, private use, unassigned) and Z (separators) other than a plain space, every default-ignorable code point, and the blank Braille pattern U+2800 is shown as a `\u{XXXX}` escape, in the arguments and in every other string an agent or the hub wrote that the overlay shows: agent names, the attach reason, toasts and their captions, cursor and highlight labels, chat. In the same strings every combining mark beyond the second in a row is shown as such an escape, and each line of the argument listing clips what it paints, so that a letter stacked with marks cannot paint over the lines around it.
- **What cannot be shown in full is not asked at all.** More than 40 object keys and array items in total, containers nested deeper than 4, a rendered listing of more than 2000 code points, or a value that is not JSON: the request fails with `E_TOO_LARGE`.
- **A tall card has to be read.** A card taller than the window scrolls and says "Scroll to the end to review everything before allowing." Allow, "Always allow" and its second step stay inactive until the person has scrolled the card to its end.
- **The page cannot change under the prompt.** While a consent prompt is showing or queued, every method that is not read-only, from every agent, fails with `E_BUSY`.

## What keeps prompts honest

- **Bounded.** One pending prompt per agent and four in total. More fail with `E_BUSY`.
- **A request's time runs from when it arrived.** The time a request has for an answer is counted from when it reached the page, not from when its card is shown, and is the shorter of `consent.timeoutMs` and the `consentTimeoutMs` the hub announced in `welcome`: a prompt never outlives the hub's wait for it. A `detach` for an agent withdraws the request pending for it, also one an app's own consent handler is still asking about.
- **Clear at a glance.** What refuses or puts off stands on the left of a prompt's foot (Deny, then "Later"), what approves on the right ("Always allow", then Allow, the one filled button), and above them one line says what happens if nobody answers. On a narrow screen the two groups wrap, each staying together.
- **After a refusal, a notice.** When the person refused an action prompt, the page shows a short notice of its own for 8 s: that the action did not run ("Denied. order.submit did not run for “Tab assistant” (a1)."), with up to two things to do about it with one click: "Block this action", which sets the rule Block for that action and agent (it makes the agent ask less of them, so it takes no second step), and, where the agent holds the `chat` scope, "Say why in the chat", which opens the Chat tab with that agent addressed. The notice asks nothing and holds nothing back: it takes no focus, has no text field, its buttons ignore clicks for their first 500 ms, it goes by itself, and it is taken down when a prompt comes up. There is none after a refused attach, nor when the refusal ended the grant.
- **Cool-off.** After a refusal, a timeout, a "Later", or a prompt the agent itself withdrew (its session left the hub, or it attached again while its prompt was up), that agent's action prompts, and attach prompts from any agent, are refused with `E_RATE` for 2 s, doubling with each further one up to 60 s. An approval resets it. So an agent cannot throw one prompt after another by having each put off.
- **Three refusals end it.** Three explicit refusals in a row of one agent's action prompts revoke its grant as Stop does, and the third request fails with `E_CONSENT`. A timeout, a "Later" and a withdrawn prompt do not count toward the three, and neither do Discard and a reviewed Deny in the waiting list.
- **No accidental approval.** Allow ignores clicks for the first 500 ms after the prompt appears or moves, and shows that it is not yet active. A pointer click on Deny, or on "Later", is taken at once: neither approves anything. The pointer answers all along.
- **Keys meant for the page answer nothing.** A prompt takes the focus, and the person may be typing, tabbing through a form or about to press Enter. The prompt puts the focus on itself, the dialog, where no key presses anything, and not on a button. A key answers only as Enter or Space on a button of the prompt that has the focus, or as Escape (which denies), and only when all of this holds: it is not a repeat of a key held down; at least 500 ms have passed since the prompt appeared or moved, since the focus landed on that button, and since any other key was pressed; and at least 3 s have passed since the last key that types (a character, Backspace or Delete, or any key pressed with Ctrl, Alt or Meta), wherever the focus was then, also before the prompt came up. Tab does nothing during the prompt's first 500 ms. While the 3 s run the card says so: "Keys do not answer this request right now, because something was just typed. Use the pointer, or wait a moment and press the key again." This goes for Deny and Escape as for Allow: a key meant for the page neither approves nor refuses.
- **The keyboard still works, and that is its limit.** A person who means it answers by the keyboard alone: Tab to the button, let the focus rest there, Enter. A person who tabs onto Allow, lets half a second pass and presses Enter has approved, whether or not they read the card first.
- **Nothing an agent drew stands beside a prompt.** When a prompt comes up, every toast and highlight is taken down and the cursor's label is hidden, and none can be put up while it shows (`E_BUSY`). What an agent says about a request is on the prompt itself, under the agent's name. The cursor's label comes back when the prompt has gone; toasts and highlights do not.
- **No timer has to fire.** Every wait named here is a time, compared with the clock when a click, a key or a request arrives: the arming delays, the 3 s after typing, the cool-off, the deadline of a prompt. A prompt past `consent.timeoutMs` is a refusal from the moment anything looks at it, whether or not its timer fired.
- **The focus comes back.** When a prompt goes away, the focus goes back to where it was when the prompt appeared: the element of the page, or the control of the overlay.
- **Nothing loosens while the overlay cannot be relied on.** The driver checks that its overlay is where the person can see and use it: in the document, in the browser's top layer, drawn at its own size, not faded, filtered, clipped or transformed by a style of the page, and what a hit test finds. While that does not hold, a click on Allow or "Always allow" is not taken. The prompt stays up and its time runs on; Deny is still taken. A click that made the check put the overlay back on top is not taken either: only a later, separate one counts. See [Human control](./human-control.md#the-indicator-has-to-stay-visible-and-usable).
- **No silent swap.** A prompt withdrawn while it is showing, because its agent detached or disconnected, becomes a "Request withdrawn" notice with no Allow button for 1.5 s before any next prompt.
- **Honest about the hub.** When the hub is unverified the prompt says so.

The indicator stays above a prompt's backdrop, so Pause and Stop work while a prompt is up. While a prompt is showing or queued, the Chat tab shows nothing an agent wrote, and `chat.say` and `chat.status` fail with `E_BUSY`: no agent's words stand next to a decision. See [Chat](./chat.md).

## Remembered approvals

With `remember: session` an approved action is remembered once its handler has run, and is not asked again under the same grant unless the hub confirms the request; an approval of such a request is not remembered. Where an approval will be remembered, the prompt says so before the person gives it ("Allow is remembered: ..."). The panel shows a remembered approval where it shows the person's rules, the indicator carries a mark for it ("1 approved"), and the person takes it back in the panel. Nothing is remembered under the level `strict` or the rule `confirm`, and a remembered approval ends with its grant.

> [!WARNING]
> The remembered approval covers that action name with any arguments. This is why only the `open` profile remembers by default.

## When the page asks even though policy says allow

The surface asks before an attach even when its policy says `allow` if the hub is unverified, or if the person has pressed Stop, or a revocation after refusals has happened, since the page loaded, or if the person has tightened something for an agent that the page cannot tell this one from. In the last case the card lists what was set and says that it stays. See [Permission levels](./permission-levels.md#what-the-person-tightened-stays).

## Your own consent handler

An app may supply its own consent handler, for example an attendant PIN on a kiosk. It gets the request as data and answers yes or no. The display rules above are those of the driver's own prompt: a handler that shows the request has to keep them itself. See [Make an app drivable](../start/make-an-app-drivable.md#your-own-consent-prompt).

## What an agent should do with the answers

| Answer | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `E_CONSENT` | The person refused or blocked the action, or the prompt timed out. | Do not ask again at once. Tell the person what you wanted and why. |
| `E_WAITING` | (0.2) The person has not answered yet: the request waits in their window with a ticket (`data: {tk, ms}`). Nothing ran. | Wait for the answer (the SDK does by default) and repeat the request with the ticket once it is allowed. Do not ask for the approval in the chat. See [Requests that wait](./waiting-requests.md). |
| `E_RATE` | A cool-off after a refusal. | Wait. The cool-off doubles each time. |
| `E_BUSY` | A prompt is up or queued, yours or another agent's, or a permission changed while the request waited. | Wait for the prompt to be answered, then send the request again. |
| `E_TOO_LARGE` | The arguments cannot be shown in full. | Send smaller arguments. Bulk data belongs in a view, not in an action. |
| `E_TIMEOUT` | The page did not answer within the hub's wait. | Treat it as a prompt nobody answered. Ask the person to bring the page to the front, then ask again. |

About `E_TIMEOUT`: a prompt nobody answers ends inside the hub's wait, as `E_CONSENT` or, where the request can wait, as `E_WAITING`. The page counts a request's time from when it arrived, never longer than the hub waits, and reads the clock when the person answers, so neither a prompt that waited its turn behind another nor a timer a background tab ran late keeps a prompt answerable after the hub gave up. What is left is a request that reached a page that did not run at all for longer than the hub's wait: its prompt comes up after the agent was told `E_TIMEOUT`. The hub withdraws an attach it stopped waiting for; an action approved on such a prompt still runs. Before repeating an action that is not safe to run twice, observe whether it ran.

## Further reading

- [Permission levels](./permission-levels.md) and [Human control](./human-control.md)
- [Requests that wait](./waiting-requests.md): "Later", the waiting list and the ticket.
- [Threats and what stops them](../reference/security-model.md#threats-and-what-stops-them): T14, T15, T16 and T31 are about prompts; T76, T77 and T83 about a request's time, the waiting list and the notice after a refusal.
- [Specification, section 12](../reference/specification.md#12-policy)

# Requests that wait

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/concepts/waiting-requests.html
Section: Concepts

> A prompt nobody answered, or one the person put off with "Later", is not a refusal in protocol 0.2. The request waits in the panel for ten minutes, the agent gets E_WAITING with a ticket, and an approved request runs once when the agent asks again.

## The problem it solves

A person who is not looking at the page misses a prompt. In protocol 0.1 that was a refusal after `consent.timeoutMs`: the agent got `E_CONSENT`, and the person never knew what it had asked. In 0.2, where a request can wait, nobody's absence refuses anything.

## As the person sees it

A prompt for an action or for an attach has one more answer, **Later**, on the left with Deny. Above the buttons one line says what happens if nobody answers: "Goes to the waiting list in N s". Later, like Deny, is taken at once: it approves nothing. Either way the request joins the page's *waiting list*, and the card goes.

- **The indicator says how many wait** ("1 waiting"). With no agent attached and a request to connect in the list, the indicator is shown for that alone: it reads "An AI agent is waiting to connect", not that one is connected, and it opens the panel.
- **The panel lists them** above the agents, under "Waiting for your answer": for each the agent, the action's name and risk (or that the agent wants to connect), when it was asked and until when it waits. Never the arguments.
- **Review** opens the request's prompt again as it was asked: the same card with the same arguments, under every rule a prompt has (the arming delays, the rule for keys, scrolling to the end, nothing an agent drew beside it). Allow there approves that one request; Deny refuses it; Later, or no answer, leaves it in the list.
- **Discard** refuses a request without a card. Neither Discard nor a reviewed Deny counts toward the three refusals that revoke a grant.
- **After an approval** the list says that the agent is told and that the request goes ahead when the agent asks again, until when, with **Take back**, which withdraws the approval the agent has not used yet.

An entry lasts `consent.waitMs` from when it joined the list, ten minutes under `open` and `guarded`, judged by the clock; an approval lasts until then too. The `kiosk` profile has no list (`consent.waitMs: 0`): a kiosk visitor is not the owner, and a prompt nobody answers there is refused as before.

The activity list shows that a request waited and what the person did with it, with the action's name and never its arguments.

## As the agent sees it

The answer is the error `E_WAITING` with `data: {tk, ms}`: `tk` is a ticket, `ms` how long from now the request waits. Nothing ran. When the person answers, the agent is told with `evt user {kind:"answer", tk, answer, a?}`: `answer` is `allow`, `deny` or `expired`, and `a` the action's name for an `act` request. An approved request is not run by the page by itself: the agent repeats the same request with the ticket, `act {a, args, tk}` or `surface.attach {s, scopes, reason, tk}`, and it runs once, without a prompt. The approval is then used up and is not remembered.

The same request sent again while it waits (the same agent session, the same action with arguments equal as canonical JSON, or the same scopes for an attach) shows no new card and gets `E_WAITING` again, with the same ticket and the time left. A ticket that is unknown, used, lapsed or another agent's names nothing: such a request is put to the person like one without a ticket. An approval outranks nothing the person or a policy says: a policy `deny`, or a Block the person set meanwhile, refuses the request all the same.

What each way in does with it:

| You use | What happens on `E_WAITING` |
|---|---|
| the agent SDK | `handle.act()` and `client.attach()` wait for the answer by default, up to ten minutes or as long as the request stays in the list, and repeat the request with its ticket once it is allowed. A refusal or no answer in time is `E_CONSENT`. `wait: false` throws the `WaitingError` at once (`ticket`, `ms`, `action`, `code`, `data`); a number waits at most that long. `handle.waiting()` and `client.waiting()` list what waits, and `on('answer', ...)` gets each answer. The same call made again is the repeat. |
| the MCP adapter or the shell tools | The error is in the adapter's words: that the request waits in the person's window, that nothing ran, how long it stays, and that the same call with `wait` (milliseconds, at most 150 000) waits for the answer and runs the request once it is allowed. `reins_act` and `reins_attach` take `wait`. A `[reins]` notice tells the answer with the next result, and the surface listing shows `waiting=N` for a page where N requests of this agent wait. |
| the `reins` command | Waits for the answer unless told `--no-wait` or `--wait <ms>`, and says that its connection, and the request with it, end with the command. |

What to do with it, as an agent: tell the person, in the chat if you are in it, what you asked and that it waits in their window, and do not ask them for the approval there. A chat message approves nothing; the card does.

## When a request can wait

All of this has to hold: the page's policy has `consent.waitMs` above 0; the page has the panel and the indicator, where the person finds the list; the prompt is the driver's own (an app's own consent handler cannot be opened again); the hub speaks 0.2, and so does the agent's own link, which the hub tells the page with `v` in `attach`; and the list has room. An agent on 0.1 could never come back with a ticket, so its request never waits, and a 0.2 hub turns an `E_WAITING` toward such an agent into `E_CONSENT` ([Protocol versions](../reference/protocol-versions.md)).

## Bounds

- The list holds at most 3 requests of one agent and 12 in all. Where a request could not join, its prompt has no Later, and with no answer it ends as `E_CONSENT`.
- A prompt nobody answered and one put off with Later move the [cool-off](./consent.md#what-keeps-prompts-honest) as a timeout does, so an agent cannot throw one prompt after another by having them put off; they count as no refusal.
- An agent's entries end with its grant, however it ends: a `detach` for that agent, a new attach of its own that replaces the grant, Stop, the link to the hub closing. Where the agent can still be told, it is: `expired` for each entry, or `deny` after Stop.
- A request's time runs from when it reached the page, never longer than the hub's own wait, and is read from the clock when the person answers. No wait here relies on a timer firing: an entry past its time is gone the moment anything looks at it.

## At the hub

The hub relays an `E_WAITING` with `{tk, ms}` and nothing else of its data; one without a well-formed ticket and time, or on anything but `act` and `attach`, is a bad answer from the surface (`E_INTERNAL`). It keeps the ticket for that agent session and surface, with the request it was given for: at most 3 for one session on one surface and 16 in all, and over either the agent is answered `E_BUSY` instead of a ticket. A `tk` on `act` or `surface.attach` is forwarded only when it is a ticket the hub keeps for this session, this surface and this request; any other is `E_BAD_ARGS` before anything reaches the surface, in the same words whether it is unknown, another session's, used, lapsed or for another request. A ticket is used up the moment its check passes, so of two repeats at once one is forwarded. An `answer` is taken only for a ticket the hub keeps, recorded as a `person` record and relayed to that agent alone. When an agent whose attach waits leaves the hub, or the hub gives up on an attach the surface did not answer in time, the hub sends the surface `detach {why:"hub"}` for that agent, and the surface drops its prompt and its entries. The [audit log](./audit-log.md) carries the ticket on the request that waited, on the repeat and on the answer.

## What it does not protect against

From the security model: a request approved from the waiting list runs later than it was asked. The person approves what the card shows, as it was asked up to ten minutes earlier; the page may have changed since, and an action whose meaning depends on what is on the page acts on what is there when the agent asks again. An app whose actions are like that should give them arguments that say what is meant, or set `consent.waitMs` to 0. And a prompt on a page that did not run for longer than the hub's `reqTimeoutMs` gets its prompt after the hub told the agent `E_TIMEOUT`; the hub withdraws an attach it stopped waiting for, but cannot withdraw a single action. See [What Reins does not protect against](../reference/security-model.md#what-reins-does-not-protect-against).

## Try it

In the [playground](../../playground.html), run the assistant and press **Later** when it asks to place the order. The indicator reads "1 waiting", the Script tab shows `E_WAITING` with the ticket, and the Wire tab the frame. Open the panel, press Review under "Waiting for your answer", and Allow: an `evt user` with `kind: "answer"` crosses the wire, the assistant repeats `act order.submit` with `tk`, and the order is placed. Discard instead, and the assistant gets `E_CONSENT`.

## For implementers

The requirements are the `WT-` entries (the surface), `WH-` (the hub) and `CT-` (a request's time) of the [requirements index](../implementers/requirements.md); the cases are in the test vectors [`consent.json`](../implementers/vectors/consent.md). The normative text is "Requests that wait" in [section 12 of the specification](../reference/specification.md#12-policy) and "Requests that wait" in [section 13](../reference/specification.md#13-hub-behaviour); the threats are T76 to T78 and T84 to T87 in [Threats and what stops them](../reference/security-model.md#threats-and-what-stops-them).

# Human control: the indicator, Pause and Stop

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/concepts/human-control.html
Section: Concepts

> The person can always see that an agent is attached, can pause it or stop it at any moment, and wins when both use the page at once.

## The indicator

While an agent is attached the driver shows an indicator naming it, with Pause and Stop when the policy enables them. The `open` and `guarded` profiles have both buttons. The `kiosk` profile has Pause only: a visitor cannot revoke the station's assistant.

Under `open` and `guarded` the text of the indicator is a button. It opens a panel with three tabs: Permissions, where the person sets how much each agent asks, a rule for single actions and the scopes of the grant as switches; Activity, the last 50 commands; and Chat. The panel opens and closes on the person's input alone: no agent and no message can open it, close it or press anything in it. See [Permission levels](./permission-levels.md) and [Chat](./chat.md).

The indicator names each agent the way every part of the overlay does: the name in quotation marks, then its session id, as in `AI connected: “Barista AI” (a1)`. A name therefore cannot pass for words of the page or finish one of its sentences, and two agents with one name are told apart.

What the person loosened stays in sight. While an agent's level is not `ask`, the indicator shows that level: a chip with its name, and a dot that is amber for `auto` and red for `bypass`. While a rule of the person waives a prompt, the indicator shows that too ("1 rule"), and an approval the page remembers is counted on the same chip ("1 approved"). New chat messages show as a count on the indicator; the panel never opens by itself.

What waits for the person stays in sight too (0.2): the indicator counts the requests in the waiting list ("1 waiting"), and with nobody attached and a request to connect waiting it is shown for that alone, reads "An AI agent is waiting to connect", and opens the panel. See [Requests that wait](./waiting-requests.md).

The indicator, like the consent prompt, lives in a closed shadow root owned by the driver and acts on trusted input only: an event the browser made for input of the person and is delivering to the control it was meant for. Neither an agent nor synthetic events can press its buttons. Pause and Stop work without the hub's cooperation: the page enforces them itself.

This keeps agents out, and events that a script makes or borrows. It does not keep out script that runs in the page itself: see [What script in the page can do](#what-script-in-the-page-can-do) below.

When the hub is unverified, because the page holds no surface key, the indicator says so.

## Pause

Pause holds every command that changes the page. While the person has paused control, every method outside the read-only ones fails with `E_PAUSED`. The read-only methods are `observe`, `read`, `state.get`, `sub`, `unsub` and `chat.read`: an agent can still see the page while it waits. `chat.say` and `chat.status` are served as well: a paused agent cannot act, and can still answer the person.

Pause also stops the cursor where it is and discards queued pointer points.

An agent that gets `E_PAUSED` should wait for the person. A subscribed agent gets `evt user` with `kind: "pause"` and `kind: "resume"`. Pause holds every attached agent.

## Stop

Stop revokes the grant. The surface sends `evt grant {kind:"revoked"}` and the hub ends the grant: the agent's next request fails with `E_NOT_ATTACHED`.

After Stop, or a revocation after three refused prompts, every later attach on that page needs the person's approval until the page is reloaded, even where the policy says `allow`.

## Checks hold across waits

A command that waited, for a cursor glide, a consent prompt, or the person to stop typing, checks again, right before it acts, that the grant is live, its scope is still on, control is not paused, no consent prompt is up (except for the action just approved) and the indicator is usable. Stop or Pause pressed during a glide means the click never happens. An action that no prompt was shown for runs only if the person's level and rules still let it run without asking, and an action the person approved does not run once they have blocked it: the later word counts.

## Real input wins

Trusted pointer, key, wheel and touch input from the person holds input-synthesising commands. Every `ui.*` command waits until there has been no such input for `human.yieldMs` (800 ms under `guarded`), then runs, and fails with `E_PAUSED` if the person keeps using the page for 5 s. A pointer move counts only with a button down.

The first such input after a quiet period emits `evt user {kind:"override"}`, so a subscribed agent learns that the person took over.

This applies to synthetic input only. App actions (`act`), the cursor and what an agent shows are not held by the person's typing. Typing in the Chat tab counts as using the page, and while the app's own code runs because an agent asked for it (an action's handler, a view's renderer, a state getter, the handlers of synthesised input), the chat's field takes no input: what such code puts into a focused field was chosen by the agent.

## The indicator has to stay visible and usable

A modal dialog or a fullscreen element covers the rest of the page and makes it inert, so while one is open the driver moves its overlay inside it. The indicator also stays above a consent prompt's backdrop.

The overlay has a style of its own: its stylesheet reads no custom property, names no font family other than the generic ones and no system colour, and fetches nothing, so a page's stylesheet cannot recolour it, blank it or swap its letters, and both colour schemes are written out in it. The host element has no `::before`, `::after` or `::marker` box that a page rule can bring back, and its `::backdrop` does not show.

Where the browser has the Popover API, the overlay lives in the top layer and is shown again whenever another element enters the top layer after it, so that it is painted last: no `z-index` of the page lies above it, and a filter, an opacity or a transform on an ancestor does not reach it.

The driver checks all of this. The check fails while the host is not in the document, is inert or does not cover the viewport; while it is not last in the top layer; while a `zoom` on it or on an ancestor reaches it, top layer or not; while a style fades, filters, clips, masks, transforms or blends it; while the page renders nothing; while the indicator has no box or is not what a hit test finds at its own centre; and, where the browser can tell (Chromium), while the indicator, the open panel or the prompt that is showing is painted over.

Whenever the overlay cannot be shown where the person can see and use it, every method outside the read-only ones, and attach, fails with `E_PAUSED`, and no click that lets an agent do more is taken. A click that made the check put the overlay back on top is itself not taken: it was made on what the person saw then, and only a later, separate one counts. An agent never works where the person cannot see that it does.

> [!NOTE]
> A page that puts `zoom` on `html` or `body`, for whatever reason, fails the check for as long as it does: Reins does not drive such a page at all.

No wait of the overlay relies on a timer firing. The arming delays, the lock after typing, the cool-off and the deadline of a prompt are times compared with the clock when a click, a key or a request arrives, because timer ids belong to the document and anything that shares the document can clear them. A timer that never fires may leave something on screen; it never leaves anything answerable or running that would not be so otherwise.

![The indicator in the corner: AI connected: “Barista AI” (a3) with a 1 waiting chip, next to Pause and Stop](https://github.com/offensiveadhd/reins/blob/main/docs/demo/5-indicator-waiting.jpg)

For the same reason the driver refuses to connect inside a frame: the page around a frame could cover the indicator. See [Policy profiles](./policy-profiles.md#frames).

## What script in the page can do

> [!WARNING]
> **Script that runs in the page's own JavaScript realm can defeat the overlay, whatever the order in which it and the driver load.** An XSS payload or a hostile third-party tag is such script. Loading the driver first does not prevent it.

What is closed is one family of attacks: events that a script forges, or borrows from a real click somewhere else, and hands to the overlay's listeners. The driver keeps the functions it registers listeners with from the moment its script first runs, reads `isTrusted` through the browser's own getter, and counts an event only while the browser is delivering it to the control the listener belongs to.

Nothing else about script in the page is closed. The driver is ordinary script in that realm: it keeps its prompts in an array and its sessions in a map, and sets attributes and reads properties through methods every script can replace. The second security review, from a script injected after the driver had attached, approved an attach and an action with no card on screen and no click (a replaced `Array.prototype.push`), put a session at Bypass with nothing shown and nothing told to the hub (a replaced `Map.prototype.get`), and reached the closed shadow root through `Element.prototype.setAttribute`. Such script can also draw its own copy of an indicator or a prompt, or simply call the app's functions.

So wherever this site says "trusted input only", "only the person" or "no agent can press it", script in the page's own realm is outside that claim. What must not happen is hostile script in the page: keep a [strict Content Security Policy](../guides/strict-csp.md).

There is a boundary where the driver does not share a realm with the page. In an Electron app [adopted with `reins-electron`](../guides/adopting-an-electron-app.md) the driver runs in an isolated world with built-ins of its own, and the page's script shares the document with it (elements, styles, timers) and none of its code or objects. What the page's script can still do there is what the page's stylesheet can do, plus three things: remove or move the host element, clear timers, and keep the person's clicks and keys from reaching the overlay at all, since a capturing listener on the window sees every event first. The first two stop commands or leave a prompt unanswered. The third takes Pause, Stop and Deny away from the person for as long as the script does it, while the indicator still shows. None of the three answers a prompt or raises a level.

The full text is "The overlay and the page" in [section 12 of the specification](../reference/specification.md#12-policy), and "Script in the page's own JavaScript realm" under [What Reins does not protect against](../reference/security-model.md#what-reins-does-not-protect-against).

## Drawing the person's eye

(0.2) A person who is working in another window sees neither a card nor the indicator. The driver tells its app how many consent prompts are showing or queued and how many requests wait, whenever either number changes (`driver.on('attention', fn)`, `{asking, waiting}`), so that the app can flash its taskbar entry or raise a notification of its own. The event holds the two counts and nothing an agent wrote: no name, no action, no reason. The driver itself changes nothing of the page for it, not the title and not the icon, and what moves the counts is bounded: one prompt per agent and four in all, the cool-off after every prompt that was not approved, and the caps of the waiting list.

What the repository's apps do with it: the Electron example flashes the window's taskbar button and puts the count on the app's icon while the window is not in front, and takes no focus ([Electron: build it in](../guides/electron.md)); `reins-electron` prints one line with the terminal's bell for an adopted app, since a debugging connection cannot flash the app's button ([Adopt an Electron app](../guides/adopting-an-electron-app.md)); the Hermes Desktop plugin raises one desktop notification with fixed words ([Claude and Hermes](../guides/claude-and-hermes.md)). The notice after a refusal is not this: it is the page's own, for the person at the page.

## What an agent writes is labelled
## What an agent writes is labelled

Toasts are agent-written, so each one carries a caption naming the agent that sent it. Agent text is inserted as text, with invisible and look-alike characters shown as escapes.

## From the app's own code

The driver exposes the same controls to the app: `driver.pause()`, `driver.resume()` and `driver.stop()`. `driver.status` is `controlled` while an agent is attached and `paused` while the person has paused it.

## Try it

In the [playground](../../playground.html), press Pause while the assistant works and watch its next command come back `E_PAUSED` in the Wire tab. Press Stop and watch the `evt grant` cross.

## Further reading

- [Consent](./consent.md)
- [Security requirements](../reference/specification.md#14-security-requirements): rules 10 and 11.
- [Specification, section 12](../reference/specification.md#12-policy)
