#### CH-20

chatRelay is off, person or on, in the surface's policy and in the hub's, and the stricter of the two applies: the hub sends its value with every attach and enforces it itself, a surface that is sent none takes it as off, and true and false read as on and off.

Tests: `CH-20 the stricter of the surface's chatRelay and the hub's applies, a surface that is sent none takes it as off, and true and false read as on and off`, `CH-20 the hub sends its chatRelay with every attach and enforces it itself: under on every agent hears the others, under off none, under person only agents the surface reported as switched on by the person`, `VEC-CHAT chatRelay has three values, the stricter of two applies, and the two old values read as on and off`, `VEC-POLICY each profile matches the section 12 table`

#### CH-23

An addressed message stays addressed: when the agent it is for leaves before it is sent, nothing is sent until the person has chosen again, and for 500 ms after the room changed Send and Enter are ignored. A message of the person the hub does not relay (beyond 5 a second after a burst of 10 for one agent, or while the audit log cannot record it) is recorded, told to the surface as chat.undelivered, and marked in the tab.

Tests: `CH-23 an addressed message stays addressed: when the agent it is for leaves before it is sent, nothing is sent until the person has chosen again; and a message the hub says it did not deliver is marked`, `CH-23 a message of the person beyond its budget for one agent (5 a second after a burst of 10) is not relayed, is recorded, and the surface is told which one with chat.undelivered`

## Sections 9, 12, 13

This requirement spans several sections of [the specification](../reference/specification.md).

#### CH-21

to: "person" on chat.say is for the person alone: always taken, at the surface and at the hub, sent and relayed to no agent whatever the room relays, and read back by its sender only.

Tests: `CH-21 to: "person" is for the person alone: always taken, sent to no agent whatever the room relays, read back by its sender only`, `CH-21 to: "person" passes the hub under every chatRelay, with the trimmed text and to and no other param forwarded; an agent's message for the person alone is never relayed to an agent`, `VEC-CHAT chatAudience reproduces every row of who hears a message`

## Section 16: Versioning

[Read section 16 of the specification](../reference/specification.md#16-versioning).

#### VER-1

No common version is E_VERSION.

Tests: `VER-1 a hello with no version in common is refused with E_VERSION`

#### VER-2

Receivers ignore unknown fields and unknown event topics.

Tests: `VER-2 unknown fields on frames are ignored`, `VER-5 an event with an unknown topic is ignored, not fatal`

#### VER-3

Unknown methods are refused with E_UNKNOWN_METHOD.

Tests: `VER-3 an unknown method is refused with E_UNKNOWN_METHOD on an attached surface`, `VER-4 an unknown method without a surface id is refused with E_UNKNOWN_METHOD`, `SF-SCOPE-1 the surface checks the grant and its scopes itself: E_NOT_ATTACHED, E_SCOPE, E_UNKNOWN_METHOD`

#### VER-6

challenge.v lists the versions the hub speaks, newest first; a peer names in hello.v the first one in that list that it speaks, the hub refuses one it did not list, and welcome.v repeats it.

> The peer MUST name in `hello.v` the first version in that list that it speaks

Tests: `VER-6 the hub lists 0.2 and 0.1 in challenge.v, newest first, and welcomes each peer in the version its hello names`, `VER-6 a hub that speaks 0.1 alone lists it alone, and refuses a hello that names another version`, `VER-6 the surface names in hello the first version of the hub's list that it speaks, and says which it speaks while connected`, `VER-11 on a hub that lists both, the SDK speaks 0.2, and 0.1 when told to speak 0.1 alone`, `VEC-VERSIONS the versions are 0.2 and 0.1, newest first, and a peer picks the first one in the hub's list that it speaks`

#### VER-7

The hub records the version of each connection in its connect record, and gives an agent on 0.2 each surface's version as SurfaceInfo.v; an agent on 0.1 gets the SurfaceInfo of 0.1.

Tests: `VER-7 the hub records the version of each connection, and tells an agent on 0.2 which version each surface speaks`

#### VER-8

Toward an agent on 0.1 the hub sends no event that 0.1 does not have: no grant event of kind scopes (the grant narrows all the same, the request is E_SCOPE, the surface changed event is sent), no user event of kind level, rule or relay, no chat event; it holds and records what they say.

> an implementation of 0.2 MUST keep to 0.1

Tests: `VER-8 an agent on 0.1 is sent no grant event for a scope switch: its grant narrows all the same, the request is E_SCOPE, and the surface event that follows is sent`, `VER-8 an agent on 0.1 is sent no level, rule or relay switch and no chat message; the hub holds and records what the person set`

#### VER-9

Toward an agent on 0.1 the hub asks no chat scope for it and answers chat.* with E_UNKNOWN_METHOD, leaves kept out of the attach result, and sends E_WAITING as E_CONSENT without its data; a surface's error otherwise reaches the agent with its data unchanged.

Tests: `VER-9 an agent on 0.1 has no chat: the scope is not asked of the surface for it, and the chat methods are E_UNKNOWN_METHOD whatever their params`, `VER-9 an agent on 0.1 is not sent kept in the attach result; what stays of the person's settings holds for its grant`, `VER-9 a surface's error reaches an agent on 0.2 with its data unchanged; an agent on 0.1 gets E_CONSENT, without the data, for a request that waits`

#### VER-10

Toward a surface on 0.1 the hub sends attach with agent, scopes and reason, and v (the agent's protocol version, which 0.1 ignores), never with chat, grants no chat there, reads no kept from the answer, and drops an event of a topic or kind 0.1 does not have, unread and unrecorded.

> an implementation of 0.2 MUST keep to 0.1

Tests: `VER-10 a surface on 0.1 is asked as 0.1 asks: the agent, the scopes without chat, the reason; chat on it is E_SCOPE and it is never asked`, `VER-10 a surface on 0.1 that answers attach with chat and with kept gets neither: no chat scope is granted, and no setting is read`, `VER-10 from a surface on 0.1 the hub takes what 0.1 has and drops the rest: no level, rule, scope switch, relay switch or chat message`

#### VER-11

An agent with a hub on 0.1 asks for no chat scope and sends no chat.* request; the reference SDK says which version it speaks and refuses a chat call itself with E_UNKNOWN_METHOD.

Tests: `VER-11 on a hub that lists 0.1 alone the SDK speaks 0.1: it says so, asks for no chat scope, and refuses a chat call itself without a request`

#### VER-12

A surface with a hub on 0.1 sends no grant event of kind scopes, no user event of kind level, rule or relay and no chat event, reads only agent, scopes and reason from attach, grants no chat and answers without kept; what the person sets holds on the page.

Tests: `VER-12 on a hub that lists 0.1 alone the surface grants no chat and reads only the agent, the scopes and the reason of attach: no level beyond ask is offered`, `VER-12 on a hub that lists 0.1 alone the surface reports no level and no scope switch, which hold on the page all the same; pause, resume and Stop are sent as in 0.1`, `VER-12 on a hub that lists 0.1 alone the attach answer has no kept; what stays of the person's settings stays on the page`, `VER-12 the same on a hub that speaks 0.2 is told: the level, the scopes in force, and kept in the attach answer`

#### VER-13

From 0.2 on, an event of a kind the receiver does not know, on a topic it knows, ends nothing and changes nothing.

Tests: `VER-13 an event of a kind the receiver does not know, on a topic it knows, ends nothing: the hub drops such a grant event, and the SDK keeps its handle`

#### VER-14

What 0.1 has and what 0.2 adds to it are the tables of section 16; on a link that negotiated 0.1 only the events, methods, scopes and error codes of 0.1 exist.

Tests: `VEC-VERSIONS what 0.1 has and what 0.2 added to it are the tables of section 16`, `VEC-VERSIONS on a link that negotiated 0.1 only the events, methods, scopes and error codes of 0.1 exist`

## Sections 4 to 16

This requirement spans several sections of [the specification](../reference/specification.md).

#### ERR-1

The error codes are exactly those of the section 6 table.

Tests: `VEC-ERR every error code the spec names exists`, `VEC-ERR the error codes are exactly those of the section 6 table`

## Section 14: Security requirements

[Read section 14 of the specification](../reference/specification.md#14-security-requirements).

#### S14-1

The hub listens on loopback only and validates Host, Origin and the remote address on every upgrade.

Tests: `S14.1 an upgrade with a Host header other than loopback with the hub port is refused (DNS rebinding)`, `S14.1 an upgrade whose Origin no configured role accepts is refused`, `S14.1 every upgrade is checked: wrong Host and wrong Origin are refused before any frame`

#### S14-2

Agents authenticate with a 256-bit secret by HMAC challenge-response; the hub proves the secret; every message is sealed with a MAC bound to the handshake.

Tests: `S14.2 agents prove a 256-bit secret by HMAC and the hub proves it back; a wrong secret is refused`, `S14.2 seal MACs are bound to the handshake: a message sealed for another session is rejected`

#### S14-3

Secrets are never in URLs or logs and are stored in owner-only files.

Tests: `S14.3 secrets never appear in frames, refusals, audit records or console output`, `S14.3 the audit file the hub creates is readable by its owner only (POSIX mode)`

#### S14-4

Surfaces are admitted by origin allowlist, and by key where the deployment requires it or holds a key for the app id they claim.

Tests: `S14.4 surfaces are admitted by origin allowlist, and by key where required`, `HS-26 a surface claiming an app id the hub holds a key for must prove it, even without requireKey; SurfaceInfo.verified tells them apart`

#### S14-5

Every forwarded request is checked against a live grant, its scope and its rate.

Tests: `S14.5 every forwarded request is checked against a live grant, its scope and its rate`

#### S14-6

The surface re-checks every request against the app policy.

Tests: `S14.6 the surface applies its own policy even when the hub forwards without c:1`

#### S14-7

Arguments are validated against a schema before any handler runs; undeclared properties are rejected.

Tests: `S14.7 arguments are validated against the schema before the handler runs; undeclared properties are rejected`

#### S14-8

No frame, argument or result can cause code, markup or style to be evaluated.

Tests: `S14.8 agent text, toasts and colours never become markup, code or style`

#### S14-9

Private fields are never read and, by default, never written.

Tests: `S14.9 private fields are never read and, by default, never written`, `S14.9 commands that would change a private control they do not target are refused: clear on an editable holding one, a radio of its group, a form reset`, `S14.9 a text field swapped in for a private one stays private`, `S14.9 private text never names another node, and a node in a private subtree is named only by data-reins-label`

#### S14-10

Consent, the indicator and its panel are isolated from the page's styles and from what its scripts can reach, and act only on input the browser made for the person and delivered to their own controls. Script that runs in the page's own JavaScript realm is outside the rule, whatever the order in which it and the driver load.

Tests: `S14.10 the consent card sits in a closed shadow root and ignores untrusted clicks`, `LV-7 no method, event or untrusted input opens the panel or changes a level, a rule or a scope switch`, `LV-24 the overlay's stylesheet reads no custom property and names only generic font families, and the host pins what 'all' leaves alone`, `LV-26 a script that replaces addEventListener after the driver loaded finds no listener of the overlay or of the watch for the person's input: it has nothing to call, and what it dispatches moves nothing`

#### S14-11

A human can always see that an agent is attached; Pause and Stop work without the hub.

Tests: `S14.11 while an agent is attached an indicator names it, and Stop works without the hub`, `S14.11 Pause holds page-changing commands without the hub`

#### S14-12

Errors carry no internals; observations are size-bounded.

Tests: `S14.12 hub errors are short and carry no stack traces, file paths or secrets`, `S14.12 handler failures carry no internals and observations are size-bounded`

#### S14-13

The audit log is append-only and hash-chained, keyed where needed, and the hub refuses attach and every audited request while it cannot record.

Tests: `S14.13 when the audit log cannot be written, the hub refuses attach and audited requests with E_INTERNAL`, `S14.13 the audit chain is keyed when the hub has an audit key: the plain SHA-256 chain does not verify it`, `AU-6 with an audit key args is HMAC-SHA256(auditKey, canonical JSON); show.toast, show.highlight and stream.open are audited, cursor.* and show.clear are not`

#### S14-14

Everything a surface reports is untrusted input presented to a model as data.

Tests: `S14.14 text a page supplied reaches the model marked as page data`, `S14.14 page-supplied names cannot break the compact tree format a model reads`

#### S14-15

A grant's level, rules and scope switches change only on the person's trusted input on the surface, and a change that lets an action run without asking only through a confirm step; nothing the person sets relaxes a deny of the surface's policy or the hub's; the hub ends a grant whose surface reports a level beyond the hub's policy and takes no rule that policy would not honour. What lets an agent do more ends with the grant; what the person tightened stays with the agent, whatever the agent does.

Tests: `S14.15 only the person's trusted input changes a grant's level; nothing they set relaxes a deny; and it ends with the grant`, `S14.15 the hub ends a grant whose surface reports a level beyond the hub's policy, and never widens a grant on a surface's word`, `LV-8 whatever lets an action run without asking takes a confirm step that names the agent and what stops asking, armed after 500 ms; what asks more applies at once`, `LV-11 a rule allow the hub's policy would not let waive anything is recorded as refused and neither kept nor relayed; the grant goes on`, `LV-6 what lets an agent do more ends with the grant: after a replacing attach, a detach and Stop the level is ask again, no rule allows and no approval is remembered`, `LV-27 what the person tightened stays for the next grant of the same agent, under whatever session id and name: Strict, the rules confirm and deny, the scopes switched off; the attach answer says so; what they lift themselves does not stay`

#### S14-16

Chat is data and grants nothing: the person's words come only from trusted input in the surface's chat tab, agent text is shown as text under the grant's name and never next to a consent prompt, agents hear each other only where the policy or the person says so, the hub relays a message only to the grant it names and records length and digest, and no message changes a level, a rule, a scope switch or a consent answer.

Tests: `S14.16 the person's words come only from trusted input in the Chat tab, an agent's text is shown as text under its grant's name, and no message changes a level, a rule, a scope or a consent answer`, `S14.16 the hub relays a chat message only to the grant it names and records its length and digest, never its text`

# Contributing

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/community/contributing.html
Section: Community

> How to work on Reins. Building and testing the repository, what its checks expect of a change, and how to add or fix a page of this wiki with an ordinary pull request.

## The repository

Reins is developed in one repository, [offensiveadhd/reins](https://github.com/offensiveadhd/reins), under the Apache-2.0 licence.

| Folder | What it is |
|---|---|
| [`packages/core`](https://github.com/offensiveadhd/reins/tree/main/packages/core) | Wire types, codec, schema validation, policy engine, flow control, crypto, RPC. Runs anywhere, no dependencies. |
| [`packages/hub`](https://github.com/offensiveadhd/reins/tree/main/packages/hub) | The broker, its loopback WebSocket server and the `reins-hub` command. |
| [`packages/driver`](https://github.com/offensiveadhd/reins/tree/main/packages/driver) | The in-page runtime: UI tree, command execution, cursor, consent prompt, indicator and its panel. |
| [`packages/agent`](https://github.com/offensiveadhd/reins/tree/main/packages/agent) | The agent SDK and the `reins` command. |
| [`packages/mcp`](https://github.com/offensiveadhd/reins/tree/main/packages/mcp) | The MCP adapter and the `reins-mcp` command. |
| [`packages/kit`](https://github.com/offensiveadhd/reins/tree/main/packages/kit) | The single entry point for browser projects. |
| [`packages/electron`](https://github.com/offensiveadhd/reins/tree/main/packages/electron) | Electron: a window as a surface over a `MessagePort`, and the `reins-electron` command. |
| [`conformance`](https://github.com/offensiveadhd/reins/tree/main/conformance) | The conformance suite and test vectors. |
| [`examples/kiosk`](https://github.com/offensiveadhd/reins/tree/main/examples/kiosk) | Brew Kiosk, the demo app, a scripted agent, and the in-tab example. |
| [`examples/electron`](https://github.com/offensiveadhd/reins/tree/main/examples/electron) | Notes, an Electron app that is a surface, and the same app adopted. Installs Electron by itself; not a workspace. |
| [`integrations/hermes-desktop`](https://github.com/offensiveadhd/reins/tree/main/integrations/hermes-desktop) | A Hermes Desktop plugin that makes Hermes a surface. Not run in Hermes. |
| [`site`](https://github.com/offensiveadhd/reins/tree/main/site) | The website: landing page, wiki and playground. Built by `site/build.mjs`, apart from the npm workspaces. |

This site lives in `site/`, apart from the npm workspaces.

## Build and test

Node 22 or newer.

```bash
npm install            # also builds
npm run build          # type-check, bundle, assemble dist/
npm test               # every test
npm run test:conformance
npm run test:package   # pack, install into an empty project, import, type-check
npm run test:electron  # opt-in: a real Electron, after npm install in examples/electron
```

CI runs all of these on Ubuntu and Windows. Tests run against the package sources, so no build is needed before `npm test`.

## What the checks expect of a change

The repository is strict about a few things, and a pull request passes more easily if you know them.

- **The specification and the wire types move together.** `docs/SPEC.md` describes the behaviour and `packages/core/src/protocol.ts` holds the wire types. If the two ever disagree, fix both in one change.
- **Every normative sentence has a test.** A meta-test in `conformance/` fails when a MUST, MUST NOT or SHALL sentence in the specification has no entry in `conformance/requirements.json`, or when an entry names a test that does not exist. A change to the specification comes with its requirement and its test.
- **The vectors are regenerated, not edited.** `node conformance/tools/make-vectors.mjs --check` exits 1 if a vector file would change.
- **The published package is tested as installed.** `npm run test:package` packs the package, installs it into an empty project, imports it and type-checks against it. The commands the README hands out are run against the installed tarball.
- **Security fixes come with a regression test.**
- **A real Electron is opt-in.** `npm run test:electron` runs the Electron checks after `npm install` in `examples/electron`. It is not part of `npm test`, and the repository never installs Electron by itself.

A change to the wire format is a protocol change: see [How to propose a protocol change](./protocol-changes.md).

## This wiki

Every page of the wiki that is not one of the canonical documents is a Markdown file under [`site/wiki/`](https://github.com/offensiveadhd/reins/tree/main/site/wiki), in the folder of its section. Each page has an "Edit this page on GitHub" link at the bottom. A pull request that changes the file changes the page.

### Add a page

Create `site/wiki/<section>/<name>.md`. The sections are `start`, `concepts`, `guides`, `reference`, `implementers` and `community`. The file starts with front matter:

```text
---
title: The title of the page
description: One sentence that says what the page is for. It is shown under the title, in search results and in link previews.
order: 45
---
```

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `title` | The page's heading. The text starts at `##` headings. |
| `description` | One sentence. Required. |
| `order` | A number that places the page in its section's list. Required. |
| `nav` | A shorter title for the sidebar. Optional. |
| `draft` | `true` keeps the page out of the published site, its navigation, search and sitemap. Optional. |

### Write it

- Link to another wiki page with a relative path to its `.md` file: `[Consent](../concepts/consent.md)`. Link to the canonical documents from the repository root: `[section 5](../reference/specification.md#5-handshake-and-authentication)`. Both forms also work when the file is read on GitHub.
- **State only what the sources say.** Every technical statement, command and number on this site comes from the specification, the security model, the README, the conformance suite or the code. Where the README says something is untested, say the same.
- **Do not copy a table or a code sample out of the canonical files.** Include it, and the build takes it from the real file every time:

```text
| method | params | result | scope |
|---|---|---|---|
| `hub.info` | | `HubInfo` | |
| `surfaces.list` | | `{surfaces}` | |
| `surface.attach` | `scopes, reason?, tk?` | `{grant, surface, manifest}` | |
| `surface.detach` | | `{}` | |

| `sub` / `unsub` | `topics` | `{topics}` now subscribed | observe |

| `ui.type` | `h, text, clear?, enter?` | `{rev}` | ui |
| `ui.select` | `h, value` | `{rev}` | ui |
| `ui.scroll` | `h?, dx?, dy?, to?` | `{rev}` | ui |
| `ui.key` | `key, h?` | `{rev}` | ui |
| `cursor.move` | `to, ms?, wait?` | `{x, y}` | cursor |

```js
import { createDriver } from '@offensiveadhd/reins';

const driver = createDriver({
  app: { id: 'brew-kiosk', name: 'Brew Kiosk', version: '1.0.0' },
  hub: 'ws://127.0.0.1:7346',
  policy: 'guarded', // or 'open', 'kiosk', or a profile with overrides
});

driver
  .action(
    {
      name: 'cart.add',
      description: 'Add a drink to the order.',
      risk: 'safe',
      params: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: { sku: { type: 'string', enum: ['latte', 'mocha'] }, qty: { type: 'integer', minimum: 1, maximum: 9 } },
        required: ['sku'],
      },
    },
    ({ sku, qty = 1 }) => cart.add(sku, qty),
  )
  .action({ name: 'order.submit', description: 'Place the order.', risk: 'sensitive' }, () => cart.submit())
  .view({ name: 'chart', description: 'Bar chart panel.' }, (data) => renderChart(data))
  .state('cart', () => cart.summary());

await driver.connect();
```
```text
usage: reins-hub [--port 7346] [--profile open|guarded|kiosk] [--allow-origin <origin>]...
                 [--config hub.json] [--token-file <path>] [--audit <path>] [--audit-key-file <path>]
                 [--surface-key <appId>=<path>]... [--require-key] [--no-announce]
                 [--agent <kid>=<path>]... [--no-surface-sockets]

--agent adds a credential of its own for one agent, with its key in that file (created
when missing): the agent then starts with --kid <kid> --token-file <path>. The first
--agent replaces the default token file; --token-file, when given too, stays the
credential "default".
--no-surface-sockets makes the socket take agents only, for a hub whose pages are all
linked in-process (an Electron app's main process).

A running hub announces itself in the user's Reins folder (~/.reins, or REINS_HOME) and
leaves a launcher there, so an agent on this machine can reach it from a shell:
  node "$HOME/.reins/reins.mjs" reins_attach
--no-announce writes neither.
```
```

The wiki pages on chat and on Electron lean on `docs/CHAT.md`, `docs/ELECTRON.md` and the READMEs under `integrations/`, which the site also renders in full. Change the text there and the site follows.

- Raw HTML in Markdown is not rendered. Callouts are GitHub's: a block quote that starts with `[!NOTE]`, `[!TIP]` or `[!WARNING]`.

### Build it

```bash
npm ci                    # in the repository root: builds the package the playground runs
cd site
npm ci
npm run build             # writes site/dist and checks every link and anchor
npm run preview           # serves site/dist on http://127.0.0.1:4173
```

The build fails on a dead link or anchor, on a resource from another host, and on anything the site's Content Security Policy would block. [`site/README.md`](https://github.com/offensiveadhd/reins/blob/main/site/README.md) has the details.

## Reporting problems

- A bug or an unclear page: an issue in the repository.
- A suspected vulnerability: not in a public issue. See [Reporting a vulnerability](./vulnerability-disclosure.md).

# What's new in 0.2

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/community/whats-new-0.2.html
Section: Community

> Protocol 0.2 next to 0.1, requests that wait in the panel instead of failing, offers on the attach card, a rule for a time, the rate cap, and what a peer on 0.1 still gets. From the repository's changelog.

## In one paragraph

Protocol 0.2 is the version this build of the package speaks (0.2.0). A hub, an agent and a page of this version still speak 0.1 with a peer that knows no other: the hub lists both in its challenge, newest first, and each link has its own version. What 0.2 adds, in the person's hands, is that a request they did not answer in time, or put off with "Later", waits for them in the panel instead of failing; offers on the attach card; an Allow rule for a time; a cap on how often an action runs unasked; and a notice after a refusal. On the wire it adds the error `E_WAITING` with a ticket, the ticket on a repeated request, the event kind `answer`, `v` on the attach the surface receives, and `SurfaceInfo.v`. The pages that explain each: [Requests that wait](../concepts/waiting-requests.md), [Permission levels](../concepts/permission-levels.md#offers-on-the-attach-card), [Protocol versions](../reference/protocol-versions.md).

The text below is the entry for 0.2.0 of the repository's [changelog](./changelog.md), as it is in the file.

## The changelog entry for 0.2.0

Protocol 0.2. A hub, an agent and a page of this version still speak protocol 0.1 with a
peer that knows no other.

### For the person at the page

- A request you did not answer in time, or put off with "Later", waits in the panel
  instead of failing: a "Waiting for your answer" list, where you review, allow, refuse or
  discard it. An allowed request runs when the agent asks again; nothing runs on your
  typing in the chat.
- The indicator "AI connected" is a button that opens a panel. For each attached agent it
  has a permission level (`strict`, `ask`, `auto`, `bypass`), a rule for each of the app's
  actions (Allow, Ask, Block), a switch for each scope of the grant, and a list of what
  the agent did.
- What you tightened for an agent stays for its next connection: the level `strict`, the
  rules Ask and Block, and the scopes you switched off. What lets an agent do more ends
  with the grant.
- A Chat tab in the same panel. You type to the agent that drives the page, and it answers
  there. What you type approves nothing: an action that needs your approval still asks on
  its own prompt.

### For apps

- A page reports what the person set to the hub, and an app can read it (`driver.agents()`,
  the events `level`, `rule`, `scopes` and `chat`).
- `driver.hubProtocol` is the protocol version the page speaks with its hub.
- An Electron app can be a surface without a socket on the page side, and `reins-electron`
  adopts a running Electron app (docs/ELECTRON.md).

### For agents

- A request the person has not answered yet is `E_WAITING` with a ticket (`data: {tk, ms}`),
  not a refusal: nothing ran. The SDK waits for the person's answer by default, up to ten
  minutes, and repeats an allowed request once with its ticket (`handle.act(..., { wait })`, `client.attach(...,
  { wait })`, `WaitingError`, `handle.waiting()`, the `answer` event). The MCP tools say in
  plain words that the request waits, for how long, and how to wait for the answer (`wait`
  on `reins_act` and `reins_attach`); a `[reins]` notice tells the answer; `reins_surfaces`
  counts what waits. The `reins` command waits for the answer unless told `--no-wait`.
- New scope `chat` with the methods `chat.say`, `chat.read` and `chat.status`, and the tool
  `reins_chat`. `reins-tools chat-serve` runs a command for each message of the person.
- An agent is told what the person set for its grant: `evt user` with the kinds `level`,
  `rule` and `relay`, and `evt grant {kind:"scopes"}` when a scope is switched. The SDK
  keeps `handle.level`, `handle.rules` and `handle.grant.scopes` current, and the MCP tools
  say it as a `[reins]` notice with the next answer.
- The tool `reins_read` returns the text of an element or of the page, and the state the
  app exposes.
- An agent with a shell needs no registration: the hub leaves a launcher in the Reins
  folder that runs the same tools the MCP adapter has (`reins-tools`).
- `ReinsClient.version` is the protocol version of the connection, and `SurfaceInfo.v` the
  version each page speaks. `reins_surfaces` marks a page on 0.1 with `protocol=0.1`.

### For whoever runs a hub

- The hub checks every ticket before it forwards a request: a ticket that is not the
  agent's own for that surface and that request is refused at the hub, and a ticket is
  used once. It relays the person's answer only for a ticket it gave, sends the surface the
  agent's protocol version with every attach, withdraws an attach it stopped waiting for or
  whose agent left (`detach {why:"hub"}`), and records waits, answers and repeated requests
  with their ticket. It keeps at most 3 tickets of one agent on one page and 16 in all, and
  answers `E_BUSY` over that.
- The hub prints the protocol versions it offers when it starts, and each `connect` record
  of the audit log has `v`, the version that connection speaks.
- What the person set for a grant is in the audit log as records of kind `person`. A chat
  message is on record by its length and its digest, never by its text.
- `versions` in the hub's configuration limits it to some of the versions it speaks.

### Compatibility with 0.1

The hub lists `0.2` and `0.1` in its challenge, and a peer takes the first one it speaks.
On a link that speaks 0.1 neither end uses what 0.2 added. Nothing has to be changed on
the side that stays on 0.1.

- **A 0.1 agent on a 0.2 hub** works as before. It has no chat. It is not told the level,
  the rules or a scope switch: a request the person no longer allows is refused
  (`E_SCOPE`, `E_CONSENT`), as a refusal always was. The hub does not send it
  `evt grant {kind:"scopes"}`, because the 0.1 SDK ends its handle on any `grant` event.
- **A 0.1 page on a 0.2 hub** works as before. Agents get no chat there, and the hub takes
  no level, rule or scope switch from it.
- **A 0.2 agent on a 0.1 hub** has no chat (the SDK refuses the call with
  `E_UNKNOWN_METHOD` and asks for no `chat` scope) and is not told what the person set.
- **A 0.2 page on a 0.1 hub** shows its panel, and what the person sets there holds on the
  page. The hub and the agent are not told, the levels `auto` and `bypass` are not
  offered, chat is off, and the page cannot recognise an agent that comes back.
- The manifest a 0.2 driver sends says `reins: "0.2"`. A manifest digest pinned at a hub
  (`surfaces.pins`) for a 0.1 build of the same app has to be pinned again.
- The package name, the WebSocket subprotocol (`reins.v1`), the keys and the token file
  are unchanged.

## Where to read on

| What changed | Where it is explained |
|---|---|
| A request that waits, "Later", the ticket, `E_WAITING` | [Requests that wait](../concepts/waiting-requests.md), [Consent](../concepts/consent.md) |
| Offers at attach, a rule for a time, the rate cap, the notice after a refusal | [Permission levels](../concepts/permission-levels.md) |
| The `attention` event, the taskbar flash and badge in Electron | [Human control](../concepts/human-control.md#drawing-the-persons-eye), [Electron: build it in](../guides/electron.md) |
| The Hermes plugin's offer, cap and notification | [Claude and Hermes](../guides/claude-and-hermes.md), [The Hermes Desktop plugin](../guides/hermes-desktop-plugin.md) |
| Version negotiation and what a link on 0.1 leaves out | [Protocol versions](../reference/protocol-versions.md), [Error codes](../reference/error-codes.md) |
| The `wait` option of the SDK, the tools and the `reins` command | [Drive it from Node](../start/drive-from-node.md), [Use it from Claude Code and other MCP harnesses](../start/mcp.md), [SDK API](../reference/sdk.md) |
| What the hub records: `v`, tickets, answers | [The audit log](../concepts/audit-log.md) |

A manifest digest pinned at a hub (`surfaces.pins`) for a 0.1 build of the same app has to be pinned again: the manifest of a 0.2 driver says `reins: "0.2"`. See [Surface keys](../guides/surface-keys.md#manifest-pins).

# Changelog

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/community/changelog.html
Section: Community

> What changed in each version of the package and of the protocol it speaks. Rendered from CHANGELOG.md.

What changed in each version of the package and of the protocol it speaks. The protocol is
specified in [docs/SPEC.md](../reference/specification.md); section 16 has the versioning rules.

## 0.2.0

Protocol 0.2. A hub, an agent and a page of this version still speak protocol 0.1 with a
peer that knows no other.

### For the person at the page

- A request you did not answer in time, or put off with "Later", waits in the panel
  instead of failing: a "Waiting for your answer" list, where you review, allow, refuse or
  discard it. An allowed request runs when the agent asks again; nothing runs on your
  typing in the chat.
- The indicator "AI connected" is a button that opens a panel. For each attached agent it
  has a permission level (`strict`, `ask`, `auto`, `bypass`), a rule for each of the app's
  actions (Allow, Ask, Block), a switch for each scope of the grant, and a list of what
  the agent did.
- What you tightened for an agent stays for its next connection: the level `strict`, the
  rules Ask and Block, and the scopes you switched off. What lets an agent do more ends
  with the grant.
- A Chat tab in the same panel. You type to the agent that drives the page, and it answers
  there. What you type approves nothing: an action that needs your approval still asks on
  its own prompt.

### For apps

- A page reports what the person set to the hub, and an app can read it (`driver.agents()`,
  the events `level`, `rule`, `scopes` and `chat`).
- `driver.hubProtocol` is the protocol version the page speaks with its hub.
- An Electron app can be a surface without a socket on the page side, and `reins-electron`
  adopts a running Electron app (docs/ELECTRON.md).

### For agents

# How to propose a protocol change

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/community/protocol-changes.html
Section: Community

> What a change to the wire format or to normative behaviour has to touch, and how versioning lets implementations survive it.

## Where the protocol stands

Protocol 0.2 is the current version and 0.1 the one before it: an implementation of 0.2 still speaks 0.1 with a peer that knows no other ([Protocol versions](../reference/protocol-versions.md)). The wire format may change before 1.0, and a version change is announced in the handshake. 0.2 was added that way, next to 0.1, and the side that stayed on 0.1 needed no change; [What's new in 0.2](./whats-new-0.2.md) says what it brought.

The repository does not define a formal process for changes: no proposal template and no review board. What it does have is a set of checks that every change to the protocol has to pass, and they describe what a complete proposal looks like. This page explains them.

## What counts as a protocol change

Anything another implementation would have to follow:

- a new or changed frame, method, event, error code or data shape;
- a change to a formula two parties compute independently: proofs, seal keys and MACs, canonical JSON, the pointer frame, delta application, the prompt card;
- a change to a normative sentence of the specification (MUST, SHOULD, MAY);
- a change to a limit or a default the specification states;
- a change to one of the 16 security requirements of section 14.

A change inside the reference implementation that no peer can observe is not a protocol change.

## What a change has to touch

In one pull request:

1. **`docs/SPEC.md`.** The behaviour, in normative words. Say what a receiver does with input it does not expect.
2. **`packages/core/src/protocol.ts`.** The wire types. The file's own rule: if the specification and the types ever disagree, fix both in one change.
3. **`conformance/requirements.json` and a test.** Each new normative sentence needs an entry that quotes it and names at least one test. The meta-test fails otherwise, and it also fails when a quote no longer occurs in the specification, so an edited sentence needs its entry updated.
4. **The vectors**, when a computed value changes. Edit the generator, `conformance/tools/make-vectors.mjs`, which computes from the specification's formulas with `node:crypto` only, then regenerate. Do not edit the JSON by hand.
5. **The reference implementation**, with its own tests.
6. **`docs/SECURITY.md`**, when the change moves what an attacker can do: a new row in the threat table, or a new entry under what Reins does not protect against.
7. **This wiki**, where a page explains what changed. Pages that include tables from the specification follow by themselves.

## Compatibility

Within a version:

- receivers ignore unknown fields on frames;
- receivers ignore unknown event topics;
- receivers refuse unknown methods with `E_UNKNOWN_METHOD`;
- a receiver reads an unknown error code in a response as `E_INTERNAL` and in a `bye` as `E_GONE`.

So a change that only adds an optional field, an event topic, a method or an error code can be made without breaking a peer that does not know it. A peer that does not know a new method refuses it; an agent has to cope with that.

A change that alters what existing frames mean, or what two parties compute, needs a new version. `challenge.v` lists the versions the hub speaks; the peer picks one and states it in `hello.v`; no common version is `E_VERSION`.

## Before you write the pull request

Open an issue in the repository and describe the problem first, before the solution. A protocol change is easier to accept when it is clear what cannot be done today. Useful things to include:

- what you are trying to build, and where 0.2 stops you;
- whether the change is additive or needs a version;
- which party enforces it, the hub or the surface, and what a hostile agent could do with it;
- what it costs in tokens: the protocol's economy is a goal, not an accident.

The security requirements set the bar for anything that gives an agent a new ability: it has to be covered by a scope, a rate, the policy, and where it matters the person's consent, and it must not evaluate anything an agent supplied.

## If you maintain another implementation

Say so in an issue. Nothing in the repository tracks other implementations yet, and a change is easier to judge when its cost to others is known.

## Further reading

- [Writing another implementation](../implementers/writing-an-implementation.md)
- [Requirements index](../implementers/requirements.md)
- [Specification, section 16](../reference/specification.md#16-versioning)
- [Contributing](./contributing.md)

# Reporting a vulnerability

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/community/vulnerability-disclosure.html
Section: Community

> How to tell the maintainers about a suspected vulnerability in Reins, what to include, and how to tell a vulnerability from a documented limit.

## How to do it

Report a suspected vulnerability privately to the maintainers of the repository, not in a public issue. Include what you did, what happened and what you expected.

That is the whole policy as the [security model](../reference/security-model.md#reporting) states it. The repository is [offensiveadhd/reins](https://github.com/offensiveadhd/reins).

## What makes it useful

Reins gives an AI agent hands inside a web page, so the questions are always who the attacker is and what they gained. A message that answers them can be acted on quickly:

- **Who you were.** The security model names its attackers: another machine on the network, a web page in the person's browser, a local process, a manipulated agent, hostile page content, a kiosk visitor, someone editing the audit log.
- **What you did.** The frames you sent, or the page, or the commands. A proof against the running code is best: the reviews of version 0.1 gave most of their findings that way.
- **What happened, and what you expected.** Which numbered rule of [section 14 of the specification](../reference/specification.md#14-security-requirements), or which defence in the [threat table](../reference/security-model.md#threats-and-what-stops-them), did not hold.
- **The version**: the protocol version and the commit you tested.

## A vulnerability, or a known limit?

Read [What Reins does not protect against](../reference/security-model.md#what-reins-does-not-protect-against) first. It lists, among others:

- hostile script inside the app's own origin, which can also read and alter the chat;
- whoever holds an app's debugging connection, and an agent with `ui` in an adopted app;
- a person who chose `bypass`, and a standing rule that covers any arguments;
- a process running as the same OS user;
- a Reins folder that someone else can write;
- a surface key that the attacker can read;
- a page that chose to run inside a frame;
- a page with no key, in front of a fake hub;
- traffic confidentiality on loopback;
- a relay that withholds the tail of one direction;
- local denial of service;
- an audit log without a key or without an external head;
- a model that is talked into a bad but permitted action.

These are limits the project states on purpose. A way to turn one of them into something worse than the document says is worth sending in. So is a place where the code does not do what the specification says: the conformance suite marks the ones it knows with `it.fails` and a `SPEC MISMATCH` comment.

## What happens to a finding

The project's record so far is in the [Review](../reference/security-model.md#review) section of the security model: which parts were reviewed, what was found, what was changed, what is left as a stated limit, and which fixes have not been reviewed again. Fixes come with regression tests.

## Not a vulnerability?

A bug, a wrong page or a question belongs in an ordinary issue in the repository. See [Contributing](./contributing.md).


---

# FAQ

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/community/faq.html
Section: Community

> Short answers to the questions people ask first, each with a link to the page that has the long answer.

## About the project

### Is Reins on npm?

No. The package is `@offensiveadhd/reins`, and it installs from Git (`npm i github:offensiveadhd/reins`) or from a tarball. It is marked `private` so it cannot be published to a registry by accident. Note that `reins-mcp` on the npm registry is an unrelated package: run the commands as `npx --no -- <command>`. See [Make an app drivable](../start/make-an-app-drivable.md#install).

### Is the wire format stable?

Not yet. This is protocol 0.2; the wire format may change before 1.0, and a version change is announced in the handshake. 0.2 was added that way: the hub lists `0.2` and `0.1`, each link has its own version, and a hub, a page or an agent that knows only 0.1 needs no change. See [Protocol versions](../reference/protocol-versions.md) and [How to propose a protocol change](./protocol-changes.md).

### What if I miss a prompt?

In protocol 0.2, where the request can wait, nothing is refused: the request joins the panel's "Waiting for your answer" for ten minutes, the indicator says how many wait, and the agent is told that its request waits and that nothing ran. Review opens the card again as it was asked; Allow there approves it, and the agent repeats the request once. "Later" on a card does the same at once. On a kiosk, with an app's own consent handler, or for an agent on 0.1, a prompt nobody answers is refused as before. See [Requests that wait](../concepts/waiting-requests.md).

### What licence is it under?

Apache-2.0.

### Which browsers does it work in?

The demo has been run end to end in Chromium, with the page served from loopback. Firefox, Safari and pages served from a public `https:` origin have not been tested. The in-tab shape needs no network access and so is not affected by loopback restrictions. See [Browser access to loopback](../reference/security-model.md#browser-access-to-loopback).

### Why port 7346?

It spells REIN on a phone keypad.

## How it works

### Do I need to run a hub?

Only when the agent is outside the browser. When the assistant runs in the page, the page hosts the broker and both sides talk over in-memory links: no process, no port. See [The in-tab shape](../start/in-tab.md).

### Can an agent on another machine drive my page?

Not through the hub. The hub binds loopback addresses only, refuses any other bind address, and rejects a socket whose remote address is not loopback.

### How is this related to MCP?

Reins is its own protocol, between an agent and a web page. The MCP adapter is a way in: a stdio MCP server with 10 tools that speaks Reins to the hub on behalf of a model in an agent harness. See [Use it from Claude Code and other MCP harnesses](../start/mcp.md).

### What does the agent actually see?

A compact tree of the elements that matter: one line per element, with a handle, a role, a name and a value. After the first reading it gets only what changed. It does not get the page's HTML or a screenshot. See [Observation, handles and deltas](../concepts/observation.md).

### What does it cost in tokens?

By the README's account: a model learns an app from a prompt card of about a thousand characters, reads the screen as a tree of similar size, and afterwards gets deltas of a few hundred. Bulk data goes to the screen without passing through the model.

### Can several agents attach to the same page?

Yes. One agent holds at most one grant per surface, and several agents can each hold one. The page allows one pending prompt per agent and four in total. The [playground](../../playground.html) has two: the scripted assistant and you, at the console.

### Does it work in an Electron app?

Yes. An app you write gets its link from its own main process, with no socket on the page side. An app you did not write can be adopted with `reins-electron` through its debugging connection, and an agent that is allowed to attach can then press anything in that window. The checks ran in a real Electron on Windows; macOS, Linux and a packaged app were not tested. See [Electron: build Reins into your app](../guides/electron.md) and [Adopt an Electron app](../guides/adopting-an-electron-app.md).

### Can I use the driver inside an iframe?

Not by default. The page around a frame can cover the consent prompt and the indicator, so the driver's `connect()` fails with `E_DENIED` inside a frame. A page that is embedded on purpose, by pages you control, opts in with `framed: true`. See [Policy profiles](../concepts/policy-profiles.md#frames).

## Safety

### Can an agent run code in my page?

No. Nothing in the protocol evaluates agent-supplied code, HTML or CSS. Agent text is inserted as text, and the cursor colour is the only style value an agent may send.

### Can an agent approve its own consent prompt?

No. The prompt lives in a closed shadow root owned by the driver, is outside the tree the agent sees, and accepts only trusted input events. Allow also ignores input for the first 500 ms. See [Consent](../concepts/consent.md).

### Can an agent raise its own permission level?

No. A level, a rule or a scope switch changes only on the person's own input on the driver's controls, which sit outside the tree an agent sees. No protocol message reaches the panel, and the driver's API reads what the person set and sets none of it. What loosens also ends with its grant: after a detach and a new attach, Auto, Bypass and every Allow rule are gone. What the person tightened does the opposite: Strict, their Ask and Block rules and the scopes they switched off stay with the agent, and it cannot shed them by attaching again. See [Permission levels](../concepts/permission-levels.md).

This is about agents. Script that runs in the page's own JavaScript realm is another matter, and Reins does not defend the panel against it: see [What script in the page can do](../concepts/human-control.md#what-script-in-the-page-can-do).

### Can the person approve something by typing "yes" in the chat?

No. A chat message is a request, never an approval, and it changes no permission. An action that needs approval asks on its own prompt, and while that prompt is up the chat is hidden. See [Chat](../concepts/chat.md).

### Is the chat private?

From other agents, as far as the person set it: an agent gets only what was said to it while its grant was live, and under `guarded` agents hear each other only once the person says so. From the page, no: the chat is drawn in the app's page, and the app and every script it loads can read what is typed there and change what is sent. And what the person types goes to the agent, to whoever runs it and to the model behind it.

### Can an agent read a password field?

No. Password, card and one-time-code fields are private automatically: they carry no value, their text is never read, and they refuse synthetic input. They stay private even if the page later changes the field's type or swaps the node. See [Privacy annotations](../guides/privacy-annotations.md).

### What if text on the page tells the model to do something?

Everything a surface reports is untrusted input, and it is marked as page data wherever a model reads it. If the model is fooled anyway, what it tries is still held by its grant, its scopes, the rate limits, the policy and the person's consent.

What policy cannot do is judge whether a permitted action was wise. A model that is talked into a bad but permitted action is on the list of [what Reins does not protect against](../reference/security-model.md#what-reins-does-not-protect-against). Mark anything costly as `sensitive` or `dangerous`.

### Is the traffic encrypted?

No. Frames are plain text on `127.0.0.1`. Authenticated sessions are sealed: every message carries a MAC, which protects integrity, not secrecy. Anyone able to capture loopback traffic can read it. See [Handshake, authentication and sealed sessions](../concepts/handshake.md).

### Has it been reviewed?

Yes, by reviewers that did not write the code, against the running code: the first version twice, and then permission levels and the panel, chat, and Electron support as they were added, each with a second review of what the first one's fixes had changed (for chat, of the part a model reads and a runner executes). The [Review](../reference/security-model.md#review) section of the security model is the record: what each review covered, what it found, what was changed, and what is left as a stated limit. The second review of the panel showed that script in the page's own JavaScript realm can answer prompts whichever loads first; that is not fixed, and the documents now say so. It also says what has not happened: the fixes that followed the second reviews have not been reviewed by someone else, and nothing was run with a model, in a real Claude Code session or against a live Hermes Desktop.

## Running it

### Where is my token?

In the token file, `.reins/token` in the folder the hub was started in, unless you named another with `--token-file`. The hub prints the file's path, never the token. The SDK finds it from any folder through the hub's announcement in `~/.reins`.

### The page asks me every time an agent attaches. Can I stop that?

Under the `guarded` profile the person approves every attach: that is the profile's purpose, and no permission level changes it. The `open` profile, for local development, allows attaches, but only when the page can verify the hub: a page without a [surface key](../guides/surface-keys.md) always asks. After you press Stop, the page also asks until it is reloaded.

Prompts for actions are another matter: in the panel you can set an agent to Auto, or give one action the rule Allow, for as long as that grant lasts or for 15 minutes. An app can also offer actions on the attach card itself, under "Without asking each time", each unticked: tick one, and Allow opens a second step that sets the rule as the grant starts. What you tighten (Strict, Ask, Block, a scope switched off) stays with that agent for as long as the page is open.

### How does a kiosk work if nobody can approve a prompt?

The kiosk profile does not ask. Safe actions are allowed, everything else is denied, and the agent has no synthetic input and no navigation. See [Kiosk deployment](../guides/kiosk-deployment.md).

### My MCP tools are listed but every call fails.

The registration holds a relative path to the token. See [Troubleshooting](../guides/troubleshooting.md#the-mcp-tools-are-listed-and-every-call-fails-with-e_auth).

# Glossary

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/community/glossary.html
Section: Community

> The words Reins uses, each in a sentence or two, with a link to the page that explains it.

**Activity.** The tab of the panel that lists the last 50 commands: time, agent, method or action name, outcome, and what let an action run. Never arguments, results or page text. See [Permission levels](../concepts/permission-levels.md#activity).

**Adopt.** To drive an Electron app you did not write: `reins-electron` loads the driver into its window through the app's debugging connection and carries its frames. An attached agent can then press anything in that window. See [Adopt an Electron app](../guides/adopting-an-electron-app.md).

**App origin.** The origin of a page on an app's own scheme, written `app://name`. `*` in an origin list does not cover it, nor `file://` or `null`: each has to be named. See [Handshake, authentication and sealed sessions](../concepts/handshake.md#origins).

**Action.** Something the app can do, declared with a name, a schema for its arguments and a risk tier, and called by an agent with `act`. See [Writing good actions and risk tiers](../guides/actions-and-risk.md).

**Agent.** An AI harness, or an assistant running in another tab or in the same page. One of the two roles a connection can have. See [Roles and trust](../concepts/roles-and-trust.md).

**Attach.** To ask for a grant on a surface, with `surface.attach`. The page decides, and under the `guarded` profile the person is asked. See [Grants and scopes](../concepts/grants-and-scopes.md).

**Attention.** The driver's event for the app (0.2): how many consent prompts are showing or queued and how many requests wait, whenever either changes, with nothing an agent wrote. For a taskbar flash or a notification. See [Human control](../concepts/human-control.md#drawing-the-persons-eye).

**Audit log.** The hub's append-only, hash-chained record of connections, grants and requests. See [The audit log](../concepts/audit-log.md).

**Always allow.** The third button of a consent card for an action. It sets the person's rule Allow for that action and agent, in two presses. See [Consent](../concepts/consent.md#the-third-button-always-allow).

**Broker.** The part of the hub that authenticates peers, issues grants, enforces policy and routes requests. It is transport-agnostic, so a page can host it too.

**Canonical JSON.** JSON without whitespace, with sorted keys and numbers written one way, so that two parties hash the same bytes. See [Manifest and prompt card](../concepts/manifest-and-prompt-card.md#canonical-json).

**Chat.** The page's one chat room, in the Chat tab of the panel: the person at the page and every attached agent whose grant holds the `chat` scope. A message is a request, never an approval. See [Chat](../concepts/chat.md).

**Chat relay.** Whether agents in the chat hear each other: the policy field `chatRelay`, `off`, `person` (once the person switches it on) or `on`. The stricter of the page's and the hub's applies.

**Confirm step.** The second step the panel shows before anything that lets an agent do more: it names the agent and what stops asking, and its button waits 500 ms. See [Permission levels](../concepts/permission-levels.md#loosening-takes-two-steps).

**Consent prompt.** The card the driver shows when policy answers `confirm`, for an attach or a sensitive action, with Deny, Allow and, for an action, Always allow. See [Consent](../concepts/consent.md).

**Credential.** What an agent authenticates with: a key id (`kid`), a key, and optional caps on scopes, origins and sessions. See [Handshake, authentication and sealed sessions](../concepts/handshake.md#agents).

**Cursor.** The agent's pointer, drawn by the driver so the person can follow. Visual only. See [Cursor and the pointer stream](../concepts/cursor-and-pointer-stream.md).

**Decision.** What policy answers: `allow`, `confirm` or `deny`.

**Delta.** What changed in the UI tree since an agent last looked: a list of `set` and `del` operations. See [Observation, handles and deltas](../concepts/observation.md#revisions-and-deltas).

**Driver.** The in-page runtime of the reference implementation: the UI tree, command execution, the cursor, the consent prompt and the indicator. See [Make an app drivable](../start/make-an-app-drivable.md).

**Exposure.** Which elements the UI tree shows: `auto`, `annotated` or `none`.

**Grant.** An agent's permission on one surface: a set of scopes and an expiry. See [Grants and scopes](../concepts/grants-and-scopes.md).

**Handle.** The id of an element in the UI tree, such as `e12`, stable for the element's lifetime.

**Hub.** The broker both sides connect to, and the process that binds it to a WebSocket on loopback.

**Indicator.** The pill the driver shows while an agent is attached, naming it, with Pause and Stop. Its text opens the panel, and it shows a level other than Ask and the person's Allow rules. See [Human control](../concepts/human-control.md).

**In-tab shape.** Reins with no hub process: the page hosts the broker, and the assistant and the driver talk over in-memory links. See [The in-tab shape](../start/in-tab.md).

**Kit.** The single entry point of the package for browser projects, `@offensiveadhd/reins`, and its bundle, `reins.js`.

**Later.** The answer on a consent card that puts the request off (0.2): it approves nothing, is taken at once like Deny, and sends the request to the waiting list. See [Requests that wait](../concepts/waiting-requests.md).

**Launcher.** `reins.mjs` in the Reins folder: a file that runs the shell tools of the installation that wrote it. See [Shell tools with nothing registered](../start/shell-tools.md).

**Level.** How much the person is asked about one agent's actions, set per grant in the panel: `strict`, `ask` (where a grant starts, unless the person set that agent to Strict earlier on the page), `auto` or `bypass`. See [Permission levels](../concepts/permission-levels.md).

**Link.** A bidirectional, ordered, reliable message pipe. WebSocket, `MessagePort` and the in-memory pair all present this shape. See [Transports and framing](../concepts/transports-and-framing.md).

**Manifest.** A surface's description of itself: its app, actions, views, state, exposure and profile. See [Manifest and prompt card](../concepts/manifest-and-prompt-card.md).

**Notice.** A line the MCP adapter and the shell tools put before a tool's own answer, starting `[reins]`: what the person set, how many chat messages wait. Never page text. See [Use it from Claude Code and other MCP harnesses](../start/mcp.md#notices-what-the-person-set).

**Offer.** An action the attach card lists under "Without asking each time" (0.2), from the app's `human.offer`, as a box the person may tick. A tick alone changes nothing; Allow then opens a second step whose button sets the rule Allow as the grant starts. See [Permission levels](../concepts/permission-levels.md#offers-on-the-attach-card).

**Overlay.** The indicator, the panel and the prompts: the driver's own controls, in a closed shadow root in the browser's top layer, taking only the person's own input.

**Panel.** What the indicator's text opens, for the person alone: the tabs Permissions, Activity and Chat. See [Permission levels](../concepts/permission-levels.md#the-panel).

**Pointer stream.** A binary channel for live cursor trajectories, with credit-based flow control. See [Cursor and the pointer stream](../concepts/cursor-and-pointer-stream.md#the-pointer-stream).

**Policy.** A profile plus overrides: the rules that turn a request into allow, confirm or deny. The hub has one and each surface has one. See [Policy profiles](../concepts/policy-profiles.md).

**Private field.** An element an agent must never read and, by default, never write: passwords, card numbers, one-time codes, and anything marked `data-reins="private"`. See [Privacy annotations](../guides/privacy-annotations.md).

**Profile.** One of three preset policies: `open`, `guarded` or `kiosk`.

**Protocol version.** What a hub and a peer agree on in the handshake, `0.2` or `0.1`, for one link. An implementation of 0.2 keeps to 0.1 on a link that negotiated it. See [Protocol versions](../reference/protocol-versions.md).

**Prompt card.** The short text, rendered from the manifest, that teaches a model to drive an app. See [Manifest and prompt card](../concepts/manifest-and-prompt-card.md#the-prompt-card).

**Rate cap.** `human.burst` (0.2): how many runs of one action by one agent whose prompt was waived go unasked within a stretch before the next call asks again. See [Permission levels](../concepts/permission-levels.md#a-cap-on-unasked-runs).

**Reins folder.** `~/.reins`, or the folder `REINS_HOME` names: where a hub announces itself and leaves the launcher.

**Risk tier.** An app's statement about an action: `safe`, `sensitive` or `dangerous`.

**Rule.** The person's decision for one action of one agent, set in the panel: Allow, Ask or Block (`allow`, `confirm`, `deny`). It beats the level and covers any arguments. Allow ends with the grant; Ask and Block stay with the agent for as long as the page lives. See [Permission levels](../concepts/permission-levels.md#rules-for-single-actions).

**Rule for a time.** A rule Allow set for `human.allowMs`, 15 minutes, instead of the whole grant (0.2). It ends by the clock, and the indicator says when. See [Permission levels](../concepts/permission-levels.md#a-rule-for-a-time).

**Scope.** A kind of thing an agent may do: `observe`, `act`, `ui`, `cursor`, `show`, `nav`, `chat`.

**Scope switch.** A switch in the panel that turns one scope of a grant off, and back on, for one agent. A request whose scope is off fails with `E_SCOPE`. See [Grants and scopes](../concepts/grants-and-scopes.md#scope-switches).

**Sealed session.** A session whose every message carries a MAC under keys derived from the shared secret and the handshake. See [Handshake, authentication and sealed sessions](../concepts/handshake.md#sealed-sessions).

**Semantic id.** The name an app gives an element with `data-reins-id`, addressed as `#name`.

**Session.** A connection's identity at the hub (`a1`, `s1`): a label, never a credential. Also the background process the shell tools keep, which holds a connection and its grant between commands.

**State.** A named piece of app state an agent may read, with a getter in the app.

**Surface.** A web page that embeds the driver. The other role a connection can have.

**Surface key.** A secret shared by the hub and a page, by app id, with which each proves itself to the other. See [Surface keys](../guides/surface-keys.md).

**Target.** How a request names an element: a handle or a semantic id, never a selector.

**Ticket.** What a request that waits is given (0.2): `tk` in the `E_WAITING` error, 22 random characters from the reference driver. The agent repeats the request with it once the person has allowed it, and it is used once. It names nothing without the agent session it was given to. See [Requests that wait](../concepts/waiting-requests.md).

**Token file.** The file that holds an agent's secret, by default `.reins/token` where the hub was started.

**Unverified hub.** What a page calls a hub whose proof it cannot check, because the page holds no key. Such a page never accepts an attach silently.

**View.** A named renderer the app offers for showing data, fed by `show.view`.

**Waiting list.** The panel's "Waiting for your answer" (0.2): requests nobody answered in time, or that the person put off with Later, for up to ten minutes, with Review, Discard and Take back. At most 3 of one agent and 12 in all. See [Requests that wait](../concepts/waiting-requests.md).


---

# Showcase

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/community/showcase.html
Section: Community

> Apps, agents and implementations that use Reins. The list is empty so far, and this page says how to get on it.

## Nothing here yet

Reins is at version 0.2 and this list is empty: no entry has been submitted yet.

What exists today is in the repository:

- **Brew Kiosk**, the demo app in [`examples/kiosk`](https://github.com/offensiveadhd/reins/tree/main/examples/kiosk), with a scripted agent and an in-tab example. See the [Quickstart](../start/quickstart.md).
- **The [playground](../../playground.html)** on this site, which runs Brew Kiosk's logic in the in-tab shape.

If you build something with Reins, it can be the first entry.

## What belongs here

- **Apps** that are drivable through Reins: a page that embeds the driver.
- **Agents and harnesses** that drive pages through it.
- **Implementations** of the protocol in another language or runtime, and tools built around it.

## How to get listed

Open a pull request that adds an entry to this page: the file is `site/wiki/community/showcase.md`, and the "Edit this page on GitHub" link below leads to it. An entry says:

- the name of the project and where to find it;
- what it is: an app, an agent, an implementation or a tool;
- which shape it uses, with a hub or in the tab, and which protocol version;
- for an implementation, which roles it implements and whether it passes the [test vectors](../implementers/test-vectors.md).

Keep it to a few factual lines. The maintainers of the repository decide what is merged. A listing describes what a project says about itself; it is not an endorsement, and nobody has verified it unless the entry says so.

# Audit hash chain

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/implementers/vectors/audit.html
Section: Implementers

> Test vectors: Audit hash chain. Shown here as it is in conformance/vectors/audit.json.

Protocol `0.2`. Covers: SPEC.md section 13, "Audit".

[Download audit.json](./audit.json): the file itself, as the conformance suite reads it.

## How to use it

An unkeyed and a keyed audit chain to verify; `args` is SHA-256, or HMAC under the key, of `argsCanonical`.

## Formula

```text
hash = b64url(SHA-256(prev + "\n" + canonicalJson(record without hash))), or b64url(HMAC-SHA256(auditKey, same input)) when the hub has an audit key; prev of the first record is ""
args = b64url(SHA-256(canonical JSON of the params without s)), or b64url(HMAC-SHA256(auditKey, same input)) when the hub has an audit key
```

## Notes

All of this is stated in SPEC 13. `argsCanonical` is the canonical JSON both chains digest into `args`.

## Fixed values

| key | value |
|---|---|
| `key` | `-iH_QbYEGjOOgX9OdllDT0Jw245dyudNBRahIpz2O5A` |
| `argsCanonical` | `{"a":"cart.add","args":{"sku":"latte"}}` |

# Handshake authentication proofs

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/implementers/vectors/auth.html
Section: Implementers

> Test vectors: Handshake authentication proofs. Shown here as it is in conformance/vectors/auth.json.

Protocol `0.2`. Covers: SPEC.md section 5.

[Download auth.json](./auth.json): the file itself, as the conformance suite reads it.

## How to use it

For each case compute `HMAC-SHA256(key, peerInput)` and `HMAC-SHA256(key, hubInput)` over UTF-8 bytes, base64url; compare with `peerProof` and `hubProof`. The third case has a non-ASCII kid.

## Formula

```text
proof = b64url(HMAC-SHA256(key, context + "\n" + role + "\n" + kid + "\n" + nonce + "\n" + cnonce)); context "reins.v1.auth" for hello.auth.proof, "reins.v1.hub" for welcome.proof
```

## Notes

b64url is RFC 4648 base64url without padding. The HMAC key is the UTF-8 bytes of the secret and the message the UTF-8 bytes of the string, as SPEC 5 states; the third case has a non-ASCII kid. Nonces and keys here are fixed stand-ins for the random values.

## cases

3 cases.

# Chat: texts, messages and who hears them

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/implementers/vectors/chat.html
Section: Implementers

> Test vectors: Chat: texts, messages and who hears them. Shown here as it is in conformance/vectors/chat.json.

Protocol `0.2`. Covers: SPEC.md section 9 (chat.say, chat.read, chat.status), section 12 ("Chat") and section 13 ("Chat relay").

[Download chat.json](./chat.json): the file itself, as the conformance suite reads it.

## How to use it

`text.cases`: trim the text (`unit` and `times` stand for a repeated unit between `before` and `after`); with `ok` it is kept and has `length`, otherwise `chat.say` answers `E_BAD_ARGS`. `statusNote.cases`: the note as it is kept, or refused. `message`: take the `valid` messages, keeping only `fields`, and drop the `invalid` ones. `audience.rows`: split each row on spaces into `columns`; from the agents in the room, the agents among them that hear each other, who speaks and whom they address (`person` for the person alone), your decision must give `outcome` and `result`. `relay`: the three values of `chatRelay`, and for every pair the stricter one. `auditDigest`: the canonical JSON and the unkeyed digest a chat text is recorded with, whatever else was sent with it. `lines`: a chat text as the `

## Notes

A length in characters counts UTF-16 code units (the conventions at the top of the spec). Trimming is that of ECMAScript String.prototype.trim. Cases with `unit` and `times` stand for the text before + unit repeated times + after. `text.cases`: with ok the text is kept, `length` is its length after trimming and `kept` the text itself where it is short; without ok chat.say answers E_BAD_ARGS. `audience.rows`: split each row on spaces into `columns`.

## limits

```json
{
  "maxTextChars": 4000,
  "maxNoteChars": 80,
  "transcriptMessages": 200,
  "readDefault": 20,
  "readMax": 50,
  "readBytes": 131072,
  "statusTtlMs": 120000
}
```

## relay

```json
{
  "note": "policy.chatRelay, strictest first. The stricter of the surface policy and the hub policy applies: `stricter` lists every pair as \"surface hub result\". In a policy file true reads as on and false as off. `toPerson` is the reserved value of `to` for a message to the person alone.",
  "values": [
    "off",
    "person",
    "on"
  ],
  "legacy": {
    "true": "on",
    "false": "off"
  },
  "toPerson": "person",
  "stricter": [
    "off off off",
    "off person off",
    "off on off",
    "person off off",
    "person person person",
    "person on person",
    "on off off",
    "on person person",
    "on on on"
  ]
}
```

## states

```json
[
  "idle",
  "thinking",
  "working"
]
```

## text

```json
{
  "cases": [
    {
      "name": "plain",
      "text": "add a latte",
      "ok": true,
      "length": 11,
      "kept": "add a latte"
    },
    {
      "name": "trimmed at both ends, white space inside kept",
      "text": "  two\n lines \t ",
      "ok": true,
      "length": 10,
      "kept": "two\n lines"
    },
    {
      "name": "line and paragraph separators are white space to trim",
      "text": "  hello  ﻿",
      "ok": true,

# Consent in protocol 0.2: requests that wait, offers at attach, a rule for a time, the rate cap

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/implementers/vectors/consent.html
Section: Implementers

> Test vectors: Consent in protocol 0.2: requests that wait, offers at attach, a rule for a time, the rate cap. Shown here as it is in conformance/vectors/consent.json.

Protocol `0.2`. Covers: SPEC.md section 12 ("Requests that wait", "Offers at attach", "Levels and rules": a rule for a time and the rate cap) and the section 12 table.

[Download consent.json](./consent.json): the file itself, as the conformance suite reads it.

## Notes

Times are milliseconds. `kept.rules` lists the actions for which the person's `confirm` or `deny` rule stays for the agent. In `sameRequest` an absent `args` is written by leaving the key out.

## Fixed values

| key | value |
|---|---|
| `maxOffers` | `8` |

The complete error code list of SPEC section 6, and numeric limits the spec states.

## Notes

# Levels, rules and the decision for an act request

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/implementers/vectors/levels.html
Section: Implementers

> Test vectors: Levels, rules and the decision for an act request. Shown here as it is in conformance/vectors/levels.json.

Protocol `0.2`. Covers: SPEC.md section 12, "Levels and rules".

[Download levels.json](./levels.json): the file itself, as the conformance suite reads it.

## How to use it

`rows`: split each row on spaces into `columns`; from the policy decision, the action's risk, the level, the rule (`-` for none) and the levels on offer (joined by `+`), your decision for an `act` request must give `outcome`, and `by` and `remember` where they are not `-`. `c1`: a request with c:1 counts as the decision in `counts`. `offered`: the levels on offer from the two `human.levels` lists (`strict` and `ask` always). `hub`: the hub's decision for an action as a surface reads it from `decisions` in attach; anything missing or malformed is `confirm`. `allowRule`: where the rule allow may be set.

## Notes

Every combination of the policy decision, the action's risk, the grant's level, the person's rule for the action and the levels on offer, with what an act request then does. `decision` is the policy's decision after step 1, that is made `confirm` at least when the request carries c:1 (`c1` gives those cases). A level that is listed although it is not on offer (auto or bypass) is in the table on purpose: it counts as ask. `strict` is taken as given.

## Fixed values

| key | value |
|---|---|
| `defaultLevel` | `ask` |
| `rowFormat` | `one row per string, columns separated by one space; '-' stands for none; 'offered' joins the levels with '+'` |

```json
[
  "strict",
  "ask",
  "auto",
  "bypass"
]
```

## outcomes

```json
{
  "run": "the handler runs without a prompt",
  "prompt": "a consent prompt is shown, or a remembered approval answers it where `remember` is yes and consent.remember is session (never for a request with c:1)",
  "denied": "E_DENIED: the policy says no",
  "blocked": "E_CONSENT: the person's rule says no; no prompt, nothing counted toward the cool-off"
}
```

## by

```json
{
  "policy": "no prompt was needed",
  "level": "the level waived the prompt",
  "rule": "the rule allow waived the prompt"
}
```

## columns

```json
[
  "decision",
  "risk",
  "level",
  "rule",
  "offered",
  "outcome",
  "by",
  "remember"
]
```

# JSON merge patch for state events

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/implementers/vectors/merge-patch.html
Section: Implementers

> Test vectors: JSON merge patch for state events. Shown here as it is in conformance/vectors/merge-patch.json.

Protocol `0.2`. Covers: SPEC.md section 10 ("an RFC 7396 merge patch"); RFC 7396 section 2 and appendix A.

[Download merge-patch.json](./merge-patch.json): the file itself, as the conformance suite reads it.

## How to use it

`apply`: RFC 7396 appendix A. `diff`: any patch P with apply(from, P) == to passes. `equal`: no patch at all; some cases differ only in null properties, which read as absent.

## Notes

`apply` cases are the examples of RFC 7396 appendix A. `diff` cases list (from, to) pairs; any patch P with apply(from, P) == to is correct, so only that property is checked. The diff of equal values is undefined (section 15, mergeDiff). Merge patch cannot express a property whose value is null: such a property reads as absent (section 10). So no `to` under `diff` contains one, and the `equal` cases include values that differ only in null properties: a patch for them would say nothing a reader can see.

# Origins: of a URL, in an allowlist, of hello.surface.url

Page: https://reins.offensiveadhd.com/wiki/implementers/vectors/origins.html
Section: Implementers

> Test vectors: Origins: of a URL, in an allowlist, of hello.surface.url. Shown here as it is in conformance/vectors/origins.json.

Protocol `0.2`. Covers: SPEC.md section 5, "Origins".

[Download origins.json](./origins.json): the file itself, as the conformance suite reads it.

## How to use it

`urlOrigin`: the origin of each `url` (JSON null: not a URL; the string `"null"`: opaque). `allowed`: whether `entries` admit `origin`. `surfaceUrl`: whether `url` may be `hello.surface.url` on a connection from `origin`.

## Rule

```text
a web origin is the serialised origin of an http:, https:, ws:, wss: or ftp: URL
every file: URL has the origin file://
blob: has the web origin of the http(s) URL after "blob:", else null
any other scheme: scheme://host[:port] from the text between // and the next /, ? or # (credentials dropped, lower case) when it fits the app-origin form, else null
entries: exact, scheme://host:* (web and app origins), * (web origins only); file://, an app origin and null only by an entry that names them
hello.surface.url has the connection origin when its origin equals it; a null connection takes any URL without a web origin
```

## Notes

Computed here from the text of SPEC 5, with the WHATWG URL parser used for web origins only. A `urlOrigin` case whose origin is the JSON value null is not a URL; the string "null" is the opaque origin. The values for file: and app-scheme URLs do not come from a URL library: Node reports "null" for both, Chromium does not.
